Xi’s Delhi visit: China’s new tone, old assumptions about India
When China’s President Xi Jinping flew into (Opens in new window) New Delhi for the BRICS summit last month, it was his first visit to India in seven years. Meeting Prime Minister Narendra Modi on 12 September, Xi said the two countries should be “partners rather than rivals” (Opens in new window) . Modi also spoke of improving ties. After years of tension along their Himalayan border, the language marked a welcome change.
But better relations do not necessarily mean a different view of each other. China and India have disputes over territory (Opens in new window) , influence and international status. Some of those differences are rooted in how Chinese leaders have understood India’s place in Asia for more than a century.
The border dispute remains unresolved. A clash in the Galwan Valley in 2020 killed 20 Indian soldiers (Opens in new window) and, according to Beijing, four Chinese soldiers (Opens in new window) . The two governments reached an agreement (Opens in new window) in 2024 that helped ease their military stand-off. Yet troops remain deployed (Opens in new window) along the disputed frontier, and negotiations over the boundary have made limited progress.
Bilateral trade reached a record $155.6 billion (Opens in new window) in 2025, according to Chinese customs figures. But India imported roughly $132 billion worth of Chinese goods in its 2025–26 financial year, leaving a trade deficit of more than $100 billion. New Delhi wants better access (Opens in new window) to the Chinese market and more dependable supply chains.
Their rivalry is not only about borders, trade or military power.
The gap in overall power is also large. In current US dollars, World Bank figures put China’s 2025 economy at about $19.5 trillion (Opens in new window) , against nearly $4 trillion for India. The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute estimates that China spent $336 billion (Opens in new window) on its military that year, compared with India’s $92.1 billion (Opens in new window) . These differences help explain why Beijing may not see New Delhi as an equal strategic competitor. But they are not the whole explanation.
In a 2024 study (Opens in new window) called “Why Is China Dismissive of India’s Great Power Ambitions?,” in the Journal of Asian and African Studies , political scientist Raj Verma argued that China’s view of India has also been shaped by history and cognitive biases. Chinese intellectuals in the late 19th and early 20th centuries often treated British-ruled India as a warning of what might happen to their own country. They described India as a wang guo , or “lost country”. China faced foreign domination and unequal treaties but was never formally ruled as a single colony in the way India was under Britain.
Verma cites an earlier scholar’s account of Mao Zedong describing India in a 1970s poem as a cow, and a Peking University annotation of the poem that says the cow has “no particular talents” and that its ambitions are futile. He recounts the 1972 conversation with Henry Kissinger when Premier Zhou Enlai reportedly dismissed India’s prospects as “ a bottomless hole (Opens in new window) ”, and that earlier the writer Lu Xun had described Indians as “inferior slaves”. These remarks were not neutral descriptions of India. They reflected attitudes shaped by empire, nationalism and China’s own struggle for political survival.
Verma also argues that China’s revolutionary leaders were sceptical of India’s largely nonviolent independence movement. They had fought Japanese imperialism and a civil war, and often associated armed revolution with national strength. But India’s struggle also included armed resistance, a history that such judgements overlooked. Nor can remarks from earlier generations establish what Xi or today’s Chinese public thinks.
The BRICS declaration reiterated China’s support for India’s aspiration to play a greater role at the United Nations, including in the Security Council (Press Information Bureau, India)
Still, the attitudes are relevant because they predate the present economic gap. As Verma notes, the two economies were relatively close in size in 1978: around $150 billion for China and $137 billion for India. China’s dismissive image of India was already established.
Manjeet S. Pardesi reached a related conclusion in a 2021 study called (Opens in new window) “Explaining the asymmetry in the Sino-Indian Strategic Rivalry” in the Australian Journal of International Affairs . He described India as a “lesser” rival in Chinese strategic thinking, but one capable of obstructing Beijing’s wider ambitions in Asia. India therefore matters to China even when Beijing does not regard it as a peer. For New Delhi, China is a central security concern. Beijing, meanwhile, is more focused on its rivalry with the United States.
A third study offers a more optimistic reading. Writing in International Affairs in 2017, Xiaoyu Pu called China’s response to India’s rise “ambivalent accommodation” (Opens in new window) . Beijing could welcome India as a partner among developing countries while hesitating to accept some of its great-power claims. Recognition, in this account, can change with political interests and the state of bilateral relations.
The September summit offers a test of that argument. Xi called for a more rational strategic perception of India. The BRICS declaration also reiterated (Opens in new window) China’s support for India’s aspiration to play a greater role at the United Nations, including in the Security Council. That language is not new, and it falls short of an explicit endorsement of a permanent Indian seat.
Now the question is whether India and China can move beyond the old assumptions that have shaped how they see each other. Their rivalry is not only about borders, trade or military power. History, national pride and long-held perceptions have also played a part. Better trade and more meetings between leaders may improve relations, but they will not necessarily change these views overnight.
Saqlain Rizve is a Bangladeshi journalist and photographer who writes and documents Bangladesh's politics, society, and its regional dynamics.

articles.title_orig: Meta Ordered to Pay $25 Billion Over Cambridge Analytica Privacy Violations
articles.title_zh: Meta Ordered to Pay $25 Billion Over Cambridge Analytica Privacy Violations
articles.content_orig:
Meta was ordered to pay $25 billion in penalties by a New Mexico court on Wednesday as part of a data privacy case that stemmed from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal from nearly a decade ago.
The penalty, revealed in a court filing, comes after a jury in a Santa Fe courthouse found in September the social media giant liable for misleading state citizens about how it safeguards and collects user data and prevents harmful information from flourishing on its services.
Although the jury concluded that Meta had more than 43 million violations of the state's unfair practices act, with each transgression carrying a civil penalty as high as $5,000, a New Mexico judge was responsible for determining the ultimate fine. The Wednesday filing showed that the state was awarded $219.5 billion, but the penalty was ultimately reduced to $25 billion.
"The extraordinary number of willful violations found by the jury, the duration and repetition of the conduct, the breadth of subjects on which violations occurred, the involvement of senior Facebook leadership, the size of New Mexico audiences reached, and the clear intentional and systematic nature of Facebook's repeated misstatements established in the trial record support the highest level of penalty allowed by the New Mexico Unfair Practices Act - $5,000 per violation found by the jury," New Mexico District Court Judge Francis Mathew wrote in the filing.
The judge added that interest on the penalty shall accrue at the rate of 15% each year until the fine is paid off in full.
"For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law," said New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez in a statement.
He added that "this penalty order demonstrates that those violations carry real consequences."
Meta chief legal officer C.J. Mahoney criticized the penalty, saying in a statement that the company is "confident" that it will "prevail on appeal."
"This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," Mahoney said in the statement. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online."
Meta previously resolved various Cambridge Analytica-derived data privacy lawsuits across the nation as part of an overarching August settlement of nearly $17 billion with a coalition of state attorneys general in a separate federal case related to child safety and mental health. But because New Mexico was not part of the settlement, the state's data privacy case that arose from Meta's Cambridge Analytica scandal proceeded to trial in September.
In 2022, the social media giant agreed to pay $725 million to settle a class action lawsuit that also sprang from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal that kicked off in 2018. That scandal rocked the Mark Zuckerberg -led company before its official name change to Meta, and focused on allegations that the political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica improperly accessed the information of 87 million users , raising questions about Facebook's data handling practices.
Mathew said in the filing that "Facebook did not conduct the comprehensive investigation that it promised" following the Cambridge Analytica revelations.
"Pressure from senior executives to keep costs down, lack of adequate enforcement resources, inadequate investigative techniques, and a desire not to create precedent for future investigations," all contributed to what the judge characterized as a "willfully ineffective" internal examination by Facebook, the filing said.
Former New Mexico Attorney General Hector Balderas originally filed the state's Cambridge Analytica-related lawsuit in 2021, while current AG Torrez oversaw the related trial.
Torrez also led his state's child safety-related trial against Meta that resulted in a March jury ruling that the social media company should pay $375 million for violating the state's unfair practices act. A New Mexico judge would later order Meta to pay $567 million into an abatement fund as part of a second phase of the case that determined the social media firm's actions created a public nuisance.
Meta said it disagreed with that New Mexico ruling and planned to appeal.

articles.title_orig: Helen Haines has lost both legs after alleged attack but ‘her heart and mind are in good shape’, husband says
articles.title_zh: Helen Haines has lost both legs after alleged attack but ‘her heart and mind are in good shape’, husband says
articles.content_orig:

Helen Haines, the Australian MP struck by a car outside her constituency office in an alleged attack on Monday, has had her second leg amputated, her husband has announced.
Addressing the media on Wednesday afternoon, Phil Haines said: “Helen is alive and she’s stable. That is the most important thing for our family.”
Surgeons on Monday had amputated Ms Haines’ left leg on Monday night after she was airlifted to hospital. The 65-year-old was struck twice by a Toyota Land Cruiser SUV outside her electoral district office in Wangaratta in Victoria .
A suspect identified as Brendan Nugent, 43 , faces three charges over the alleged attack on the Independent MP, as police consider bringing additional charges against him. He remained silent during his first court appearance earlier on Wednesday.
Providing an update to the media on behalf of their family, Mr Haines said his wife’s road to “recovery will be long and difficult, but we know she is a fighter.
“She is a determined person who will do her best with our support and love to recover. And that is what we hope for.
“Her heart is huge. She is a very compassionate, caring, loving person, incredibly supportive of all around her; her family, her community, anybody she comes across and her mind.
“We are grateful and thankful that, at this stage, both her heart and her mind are in good shape.”
He said that the couple will celebrate their 40th anniversary in November and, in the last four months, have welcomed four grandchildren.
Thanking the public for the support that has been extended to the family, Mr Haines paid special tribute to first responders at the scene of the alleged attack on Monday, including police, paramedics and the members of the community.
“One thing I’ve learned in the last two days, reinforced by many people, is to take things day by day. I know it’s a cliche, but it’s a cliche for a very good reason.
“So I thank you all for being here. I thank you for listening. And please keep sending Helen your love and our family as well.”
Australia’s governor-general Sam Mostyn said she was “touched” to be invited by Mr Haines to attend the press conference, and also expressed gratitude towards the first responders.
She reiterated that Ms Haines’ recovery would be taken “day by day” after what she described as Monday’s “violent attack”.
She called on Australians to “do what I imagine Helen would be doing if she was not the victim of this terrible attack” and to “not descend into violence and chaos and division”.
The incident has shocked Australia , a country where political violence is rare and politicians have always been accessible to the public. Most MPs and even senior ministers go about their work and personal lives without being accompanied by security teams.
Prime minister Anthony Albanese, who characterised the attack as deliberate, called for a calming of political rhetoric in the wake of the incident, and thanked bystanders for intervening . He also spoke with local barber Ricky Jefferies, who helped detain the suspect .

articles.title_orig: Airbnb Hosts Are Furious They Can No Longer Make Guests Do Their Chores
articles.title_zh: Airbnb Hosts Are Furious They Can No Longer Make Guests Do Their Chores
articles.content_orig:
Airbnb is changing its house rules, including limiting the cleaning tasks hosts can ask guests to complete during their stay.
Under the new policy, which applies to reservations booked on or after Nov. 20, hosts generally will no longer be allowed to require guests to strip beds, wash and put away dishes or take trash offsite, the company announced on its website .
Hosts can still ask guests to complete simpler tasks, such as placing used dishes in the sink.
"House rules help guests understand what hosts expect, but we've heard from our community that they can be confusing, onerous and hard to manage," Airbnb said in a statement. "So we've redesigned them to make them easier to discover and clearer to set, alongside a new policy that keeps requests reasonable, with no surprises."
The new policy also prohibits hosts from imposing their own fines on guests and limits the use of separate contracts to certain circumstances, including when required by law or homeowners association rules.
Airbnb said hosts can now choose from seven standard house rules and add their own reasonable requests.
The rules will also be displayed more prominently on Airbnb listings, in guests' Trips tabs and in reservation reminders.
Hosts can continue to update their house rules at any time. If a request does not follow the policy, Airbnb said it will flag the issue and allow hosts to appeal.

articles.title_orig: US adds wrongful detention warning to China travel advisory - VOA
articles.title_zh: US adds wrongful detention warning to China travel advisory - VOA
articles.content_orig:
Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Mandarin article .
The U.S. State Department has added a wrongful detention warning to its travel advisory for mainland China, cautioning that Americans face a serious risk of being detained without a fair legal process.
The advisory, updated October 19, keeps China at Level 2 — “Exercise Increased Caution” but adds a “D” risk indicator for wrongful detention. The advisory warns that Chinese authorities may enforce local laws arbitrarily and impose exit bans without a fair and transparent legal process.
In an emailed statement to VOA, the State Department said it had determined that “Americans are at serious risk of wrongful detention in China.”
“The Trump Administration has no higher priority than the safety and security of Americans,” a State Department spokesperson told VOA, adding that the administration was committed to securing the release of Americans wrongfully detained overseas.
The department identifies several groups that may face heightened risks, including Americans of Chinese descent, people involved in business disputes, and those with current or past ties to U.S. law enforcement, the military, intelligence agencies or the federal government.
The House Select Committee on China called the new “D” indicator “a serious warning to all Americans” in a social media post Tuesday.
Wrongfully detained Americans
The State Department has formally designated two U.S. citizens detained in China as wrongfully detained: Chinese American seismologist Chen Youlin and Myanmar-born American scholar Min Zin.
Chen had worked with Chinese researchers on a U.S. government-funded public research project examining seismic signals from underground nuclear tests in North Korea.
Chinese authorities arrested Chen on November 5, 2024, as he prepared to return to the United States after visiting family in China. On May 1, 2025, China accused him of espionage. The State Department designated his case as wrongful detention in March 2026.
Min Zin, who studies Myanmar politics and China-Myanmar relations, was detained by Chinese authorities after traveling to China’s southern Yunnan province for a conference in June this year. Beijing accused him of suspected espionage that endangered China's national security. The State Department designated his case as wrongful detention on August 20.
The designations make securing the release of both men a U.S. government priority.
Families urge more pressure
President Donald Trump said he raised the cases of detained Americans and Chinese political prisoners with Chinese President Xi Jinping during their White House meeting at the end of September.
The State Department also confirmed to VOA that Washington had directly raised Chen's and Min Zin's cases with Beijing.
Chen's wife, Rong Yufang, welcomed the updated travel advisory in a written statement sent to VOA through Global Reach, a nonprofit organization working to secure her husband's release.
“I am grateful to Secretary Rubio for taking this action,” she said. “He has tried for months to quietly resolve my husband’s wrongful detention in China, and President Trump has even asked President Xi twice about Youlin.”
Aung Maw Zin, Min Zin’s brother, told VOA on Wednesday that “we are glad to see this small but important step that could help ensure that no other American family has to endure the nightmare our family has been living through since June.”
The United States previously placed China at Level 3, with a “D” indicator for wrongful detention. The advisory was downgraded to Level 2 and the indicator removed on November 27, 2024, after three Americans detained in China for years were released in a prisoner exchange between Washington and Beijing.
Upcoming summits could bring renewed pressure
Eric Lebson, chief strategy officer at Global Reach, told VOA that the espionage allegations against Chen were fabricated.
Lebson said Trump could press for a resolution when he meets Xi at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen and the G20 meeting at Mar-a-Lago over the next two months.
“President Xi can expect President Trump to continue raising the need to resolve this case while the State Department increases the costs associated with holding two U.S. citizens,” Lebson said.
Beijing has rejected allegations of wrongful detention, maintaining that its judicial authorities handle cases in accordance with the law. The Chinese Embassy in Washington has yet not responded to VOA's request for comment.

articles.title_orig: IBM Stock Rallies as Earnings Offer Glimmer of Recovery
articles.title_zh: IBM Stock Rallies as Earnings Offer Glimmer of Recovery
articles.content_orig:
IBM shares slipped in extended trading on Wednesday after the technology vendor reported better-than-predicted third-quarter results.
Here's how the company performed relative to LSEG consensus:
IBM's revenue grew about 5% from a year ago, according to a statement . Net income, at $2.19 billion, or $2.30 per share, increased from $1.74 billion, or $1.84 per share, a year ago. Adjusted earnings exclude acquisition-related adjustments.
"Our clients are now deploying 'Super Intelligence' in ways that transform entire operating models, instead of simply addressing narrow or novel problems," IBM CEO Arvind Krishna was quoted as saying in a statement.
With respect to guidance, IBM called for full-year free cash flow to increase by more than $1 billion. The forecast as of July was a bump of approximately $1 billion. IBM still sees 2026 constant-currency revenue growth between 4% and 5%.
In the third quarter, IBM generated $7.80 billion in software revenue, growing 8% and topping the $7.66 billion consensus among analysts polled by StreetAccount.
Consulting revenue, at $5.34 billion, was flat and just below StreetAccount's $5.37 billion consensus.
"AI is increasingly embedded in broader transformations our clients are undertaking, representing about 30% of our consulting revenue in the quarter and 35% of our backlog," Jim Kavanaugh, IBM's finance chief, said on a conference call with analysts.
The consulting unit's 27.4% gross margin narrowed from 28.9% in the second quarter.
"We reinvested productivity gains into digital assets, accelerating our transition towards a services as software model to capture the growing AI opportunity," Kavanaugh said.
Infrastructure revenue came to $3.70 billion. That was up 4% and higher than the $3.57 billion consensus from StreetAccount.
The company's adjusted gross margin, at 58.5%, was narrower than the StreetAccount consensus of 59.1%.
During the quarter, IBM said it agreed to buy Boeing and General Motors' HRL Laboratories , formerly known as Hughes Aircraft's research division, for an undisclosed sum.
As of Wednesday's close, IBM stock has come down 15%, while the S&P 500 index has gained 13%.
"I think the current street estimates for the year are about $32 billion of revenue," Kavanaugh said. "We feel comfortable with that $32 billion of revenue."

articles.title_orig: Meta earnings live: Meta beats Q3 revenue expectations, announces 2-for-1 stock split
articles.title_zh: Meta earnings live: Meta beats Q3 revenue expectations, announces 2-for-1 stock split
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Meta ( META ) kicked off Big Tech's earnings season after the bell Wednesday, beating expectations on revenue, but GAAP earnings per share took a hit as a result of legal fees related to its teen mental health settlement.
The company also announced a 2-for-1 stock split, giving each owner of Class A Meta shares a non-voting Class C share.
The move will allow Meta to ensure CEO Mark Zuckerberg retains overall control of the company, while allowing it to continue to finance its AI buildout.
Revenue for the quarter was an all-time high of $64 billion, well ahead of the $63.3 billion analysts were anticipating. GAAP earnings per share came in at $3.83 versus expectations of $3.56, but would have been $7.40 without the legal charge.
The company saw EPS of $1.05 and revenue of $51.2 billion in Q3 last year.
Meta also narrowed its capital expenditure projections, raising the bottom line from between $130 billion and $145 billion to between $135 billion and $145 billion.
It was more than a year ago that … I wrote the letter of personal superintelligence as the North Star for the work that we're doing here.
The most important thing that we can build for this next generation of technology is basically putting this technology in everyone's hands, which is the personal superintelligence vision …
These are long-term bets. I feel like this is what we're here to do: make long-term technology bets and design the best experiences end to end that we can for billions of people around the world.
And I think as long as we continue to do that, then over time the business takes care of itself.
Ads business has been benefiting for many years from ongoing investments in traditional AI machine learning models and continues to improve thanks to the more recent generation of models.
Meta CFO Susan Li says that the company is poised to take on the enterprise market thanks to AI.
"AI is creating huge amounts of disruption in enterprise today. We really don't believe that traditional enterprise companies have this locked down.
Some of the leading companies in this space today didn't exist a few years ago. Those companies made large investments in model development and we've done the same, and we have increasingly competitive models to bring to bear.
We expect that this will be an opportunity that will develop over mutlple years and we intend to scale our investment behind demonstrated customer demand and product market fit in this area."
Meta says that its enterprise offerings via its Muse AP, Muse code, and business agents are growing quickly.
Meta's Muse AI agent is one of the most talked-about topics on the company's earnings call.
CEO Mark Zuckerberg says 10 million people in the US and Canada have set up the app.
The company is working to optimize compute efficiency to roll it out globally, and expects to eventually have more than one billion people on the service.
Meta's Mark Zuckerberg will stay in California as part of the company's Class C stock agreement and to remain close to the company's Meta Superintelligence Labs.
Initial reports indicated he could leave if Proposition 40 passes in the state. The measure, which is on the November ballot, calls for a 5% tax on taxpayers with assets over $1 billion.
Meta CFO Susan Li told investors that the company's use of predictive AI models is helping it better understand users and deliver ad experiences more closely aligned with their unique preferences.
Meta CFO Susan Li said global time spent per user on Instagram increased to an all-time high in Q3.
Facebook's Reels also reached an all-time high in both the US and globally, and time spent on Threads increased by 20% year over year.
Zuckerberg says Meta's Reality Labs losses will decline as it seeks to pace the release of virtual reality headsets in favor of focusing on personal superintelligence.
"We expect P&L of Reality Labs to improve from here, with operating loss coming down to around $15 billion next year, and trending toward profitability from there," he said.
Meta's Mark Zuckerberg says that the company believes that its Muse AI agent will become the most important part of its smart glasses strategy.
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg says that Meta expects Muse compute cost efficiency to improve by 10x in the next year.
"If compute efficiency continues to improve quickly for another few years, which we think is highly likely, then Muse will be highly profitable over multiple years."
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg says Meta expects Muse to serve billions of people.
While average revenue per American user for existing family of apps users is several hundreds of dollars, he says he expects Muse to be higher.
The most common use case for Muse is shopping. The average purchase size is over $200.
Plaid told Meta that it hadn't seen activity like it had seen using Muse's connector.
Outside of shopping, personal productivity and connecting Muse to other services are the leading use cases.
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg took a shot at Elon Musk's X during the company's third quarter earnings call, saying that Meta's Threads platform has overtaken X in terms of monthly active users.
Meta narrowed the range of its full-year 2026 capital expenditures, raising the lower end of its projections.
The company now expects to spend between $135 billion and $145 billion from between $130 billion and $145 billion.
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg says he may move out of California if the state's Proposition 40 passes.
The measure, which seeks to impose a 5% tax on taxpayers with assets over $1 billion, will be on the state's Nov. 3 ballot.
In addition to all-time-high revenue, Meta said it's creating a new class of non-voting stock.
The Class C shares will be distributed to existing stockholders and begin trading in late January 2027.
The structure is designed to allow Meta to raise capital for its continued AI build-out, while ensuring CEO Mark Zuckerberg retains control of the company.
Meta stock rose following its Q3 results, rising more than 3% after the company reported all-time revenue results.
GAAP earnings per share took a hit due to Meta's teen mental health settlement, coming in at $3.83. It would have been $7.40 without the fee.
"This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," C.J. Mahoney, Meta's chief legal officer, said in a statement.
"At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online. We are confident we will prevail on appeal. In the meantime, Meta will continue to build a safe and free platform to connect millions of Americans, grow small businesses, and help the country maintain its competitive edge."
Meta's Muse has amassed 10.9 million downloads since its launch on Sept. 8, according to newly released data from Sensor Tower. Muse has received more than 10.2 million downloads from the US alone. In contrast, US downloads for OpenAI's ( OPAI.PVT ) ChatGPT in the past 30 days have declined by 25% over the prior 30-day period.
Sensor Tower estimated that Muse reached 2.5 million daily active users (DAUs) for the first time on Oct. 16, as DAUs increased 15% week over week for the past seven days. Read more .

articles.title_orig: SpaceX and Tesla Consider Merger
articles.title_zh: SpaceX and Tesla Consider Merger
articles.content_orig:
Tesla reported better-than-expected third-quarter results after the bell on Wednesday, even as automotive revenue dropped. The stock was little changed in extended trading.
Here's how the company did, compared with estimates from analysts polled by LSEG:
Tesla's earnings report lands a day after CEO Elon Musk told investors on SpaceX's quarterly call that it would be a "good idea" for his two companies to merge, and said the boards at both have formed special committees to discuss a possible tie-up.
"I feel like I'm tap dancing through a minefield," Musk said on the call, responding to a question about a potential merger.
"Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes," Musk said. "But at the end of the day, the shareholders have to be supportive of this." On the Tesla side, that means needing a 50% vote of all shares, which is "quite a high hurdle," he said.
Musk addressed the matter in his opening comments on the Tesla call, but didn't provide any additional information.
"I think I said everything that should be said yesterday," Musk said.
Tesla's revenue was down slightly flat from a year earlier, when the company generated sales of $28.24 billion, Tesla said in its earnings deck. In Tesla's core automotive business, revenue declined 3% from a year earlier to $20.56 billion in the quarter. Energy revenue fell 16% to $2.88 billion.
Balancing out the declines were gains in Tesla's services and other revenue. Sales there climbed 33% from a year ago to $4.61 billion.
Tesla blamed its lackluster automotive revenue and profits on lower average sales prices for its cars during the quarter, and trouble securing battery supplies to make enough vehicles to fulfill a backlog of orders.
Net income attributable to common share holders plummeted 29% to $787 million, or 22 cents a share, from $1.11 billion, or 32 cents a year earlier, Tesla said.
The drop in profitability reflects a surge in spending on Optimus humanoid robots and other artificial intelligence initiatives. Capital expenditures more than doubled from a year earlier to $3.73 billion. Free cash flow plunged by 62% year over year to $1.53 billion, after Tesla turned free cash flow negative in the second quarter.
Tesla said uptake of its FSD (Supervised), a partially automated driving system the company sells for $99 per month in the U.S., grew by 20 percentage points from the second quarter. Active FSD subscriptions increased 67% from a year earlier to 1.74 million.
"We believe that FSD is driving demand in markets where it is available, and we continue to work with regulators to get it approved in other markets," the company said in its investor deck.
Ashok Elluswamy, Tesla's vice president of Autopilot, said on the earnings call that the company plans to give some customer cars access to FSD (Unsupervised) around the second quarter of next year.
Tesla is testing its Cybercab, a bronze two-seater designed for use as a robotaxi, but that's not yet sold to individuals. Musk said on the call that "the vast majority of the Cybercab stuff will be essentially Tesla-owned and transport-as-a-service."
The company plans to bring Cybercab in cities beyond Austin, Texas, this year, Taneja said, paying attention to operating costs like maintenance, charging and cleaning.
In response to a question on the call, Musk said the Robotaxi fleet, which includes Cybercabs, will start to contribute to the company's financials in 2027.
"It's not like going to move the needle this quarter," Musk said, "I think it starts to become noticeable in Q2 and then probably a big deal by Q3 or Q4 of next year."
Barring regulatory intervention and protectionism, "Tesla will end up doing a majority of all passenger miles on Earth in any country where it is allowed to operate freely."
Tesla said its auto sales in Canada, Japan, Taiwan and Australia hit new records during the quarter. However, the company has gotten meager growth out of its core market of late as Chinese EV makers such as BYD and Xiaomi gained popularity in Asia and Europe with affordable and innovative EVs. Tesla was also hit last year by the end of a federal EV tax credit.
Earlier this month, Tesla reported vehicle deliveries for the third quarter of 486,532, about 2% below the year-ago number. Deliveries are the closest approximation of sales reported by Tesla but are not precisely defined in its shareholder communications.
One of Tesla's big investments is in a semiconductor factory that it's building with SpaceX and Intel in Grimes County, Texas. That partnership with SpaceX along with other areas of overlap, including work on Tesla's recently announced Roadster refresh, fueled intensifying speculation that Musk's companies were on the verge of combining in what would be a historic transaction.
On Optimus, Musk said Tesla is "making good progress" on the AI systems that control the robots in development. He said there's "still quite a lot of work to do with regard to the AI and the robot for it to be truly useful for open-ended tasks."
Musk said he expects current issues around electromechanical design, reliability, usage duration, and AI to be "solved around the end of next year."

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo will not require further treatment after lung surgery, doctors say
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo will not require further treatment after lung surgery, doctors say
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo XIV will not need further treatment following lung cancer surgery , his doctors said Wednesday.
The Vatican’s press office released an update from the pontiff’s doctors, saying final reports and analyses of tissue removed from his surgery were completed Wednesday.
Pope Leo rides popemobile for first time since surgery
“The results have confirmed that the condition was a pulmonary adenocarcinoma and that the disease was localized,” said his doctors, Dr. Luigi Carbone and Prof. Stefano Margaritora.
“A subsequent oncological evaluation has confirmed that no further therapy is required,” the statement said.
The 71-year-old American had surgery earlier this month at Rome’s Gemelli Hospital to remove a lung nodule found during recent routine medical tests. Leo said the nodule was detected “at a very early stage.”
He was discharged on Saturday and returned to his public duties on Sunday with a prayer from the window of the papal apartment at St. Peter’s Basilica.
“This experience has made me feel particularly close to all those who are experiencing illness and a condition of frailty,” he said, thanking well-wishers.
Leo said that “having come through this delicate phase, as you know, I will now gradually resume my activities, always with God’s help and your prayers.”
The pope’s diagnosis and surgery left his upcoming trip to South America up in the air. He is still scheduled to depart on Nov. 6 for the 12-day journey to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.
The trip will be a demanding one, covering 19,000 miles on multiple flights and two helicopter rides. His itinerary includes a stopover in Cuzco in the Peruvian Andes that sits at an elevation of 11,000 feet.
Peru is a special place for Pope Leo, where he formerly served as bishop of Chiclayo and holds citizenship.
The pope’s surgeon, Margaritora, on Saturday told Vatican News that recovery from Leo’s type of surgery typically takes a couple of weeks.
“As for a long trip involving air travel in about three weeks, I would say there are no clinical reasons why it should not take place,” Margaritora said.
Marlene Lenthang is a breaking news reporter for NBC News Digital.
Claudio Lavanga is Rome-based foreign correspondent for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: U.S. reducing troop footprint in Middle East, sources say, as indirect talks on ceasefire proposal with Iran continue
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: U.S. reducing troop footprint in Middle East, sources say, as indirect talks on ceasefire proposal with Iran continue

A U.S. official and a senior U.S. military official told CBS News on Wednesday the military has been quietly reducing its footprint at posts in the Middle East due to ongoing regional threats from the Houthis and direct threats from Iran.
NBC News was first to report on the drawdowns.
Asked about the reports, U.S. Central Command spokesperson Capt. Tim Hawkins told CBS News: "We regularly move U.S. service members and assets to optimize mission readiness. We do not discuss related movements for operational security reasons. U.S. forces remain vigilant and ready to protect American personnel and interests across the region."
The U.S. State Department has also ordered non-essential U.S. embassy personnel and their families to depart Saudi Arabia, citing threats posed by the Iran-backed Houthis.
CBS News has learned several U.S. embassies in the Middle East have adjusted their staffing under "restricted operations" status.
The restricted operations status, which the department introduced in August amid flare-ups in the war with Iran, allows embassies to reduce staffing and services without fully suspending operations.
The Saudi energy ministry said that falling debris from the interception of a drone targeting an oil facility killed two people and injured two others on Wednesday.
"The attempted attack resulted in the deaths of two individuals, a Filipino and a Nepali, and injuries to two others," the ministry said in a statement. It did not say who launched the drone aimed at the Shaybah oil field near the UAE border.
The U.S. has ordered all non-emergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia as the kingdom faces escalating attacks by Houthi militants.
"Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions," State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said in a social media post Wednesday.
The order came a few days after the U.S. embassies in Saudi Arabia , Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and several other countries warned that hostilities could rapidly and without warning spread beyond areas already affected by the fighting.
"The safety and security of Department personnel and their families remain our highest priority, and we will continue to take all necessary steps to protect and support them," Pigott added.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi issued a warning to the U.S. on Wednesday afternoon, saying it should choose diplomacy over returning to war.
"Iran is prepared to give diplomacy another chance if we see strong evidence of a sincere desire by US to build trust & reach a just solution," he wrote on X , sharing a link to an opinion piece in the Financial Times. "But if US chooses war over diplomacy, it'll certainly result in an even greater strategic failure."
Araghchi said earlier in the day that Iran and the U.S. were still involved in indirect negotiations via mediators over the seven-day ceasefire proposal from September. The proposal was outright rejected by President Trump, but Araghchi said the U.S. was trying to add further clauses to the agreement.
The U.S. Treasury announced new sanctions on the Panamanian-Greek law firm Karnakis and Karnakis for involvement in Iran's "shadow fleet" as part of its Operation Economic Outcast .
The U.S. accuses Karnakis and Karnakis of being indirectly involved in Iran's illicit shipping operations for years. A "shadow fleet" refers to oil tankers that hide their true ownership in order to evade sanctions.
"Whether you are conducting illegal oil transfers at sea or sitting in the corner office of a law firm, if you are supporting the Iranian regime, we will find you and sanction you," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement. "Iran's facilitators must make a choice: Either you are with us or against us. We know who you are, we know what you're doing, and we will continue to take action."
The Treasury also said it sanctioned Singapore- and UAE-based shipping agents, including a fleet of cargo vessels that has directly taken part in Iran's "shadow fleet" and "helped generate substantial revenue for the Iranian regime."
A limited number of Saudi airlines took off and landed at the country's main airport on Wednesday, two days after authorities notified airlines that they could resume operations with prior permission.
Saudia and FlyNas were operating flights Wednesday, according to flight-tracking data published by FlightAware. Major carriers, including Lufthansa and Air France, have canceled flights through mid-November.
Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport has been hit multiple times this month by Yemen's Houthi rebels and shut down on Oct. 10. A strike two weeks ago killed 13 people and injured hundreds more.
The Houthis have acknowledged attacking the airport, claiming without evidence that Saudi Arabia provided military equipment to government forces through the facility.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said any interference in the Yemen war by Egypt or any other country would make the situation "more difficult."
"Egypt has sufficient experience to avoid entangling itself in such a highly complex conflict," said Iran's top diplomat in an interview with Iraqi state broadcaster Al-Iraqiya aired on Tuesday.
"We believe that any foreign presence or interference will only make resolving this issue more difficult," Araghchi noted.
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said on Wednesday that Cairo's proposed military support for Riyadh was to "defend Saudi territory, and does not include an attack on Yemen," according to a statement from his office.
At a government event titled Egypt Forum 2026, Sisi said the "objective is to defend the kingdom's lands and borders, as well as those of any other Arab state, should it be requested of Egypt," his spokesman said in a statement.
Sisi on Saturday had asked parliament to authorize support for Saudi Arabia in its war with the Houthis, "if requested."
The parliament, which is stacked with supporters of the president, has since held two rare secret sessions, before postponing deliberations until next week.
Iran's newly appointed defense minister, Mehrdad Akhlaghi, said Wednesday his first hours in office were devoted to meeting the requirements of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' Aerospace Force and the army's air defense units.
"We are not in a war of rhetoric in response to repeated threats; we are turning threats into greater readiness and more effective defensive power," he wrote in his first post on X since taking office.
Akhlaghi added Iran was concentrating on its objectives through the use of new technologies.
"We may eat dirt, but we will not give up our soil," he concluded.
President Trump blocked a planned Israeli multiday operation that would have resumed strikes against Iran on the weekend of Oct. 10, according to the Financial Times .
The plan was designed to exceed the intensity of the joint U.S.-Israeli military offensive launched in February, three people familiar with the matter told the paper, and would have struck Iranian nuclear sites, regime targets and civilian infrastructure such as power plants.
The president blocked the strike to avoid escalating conflict before the U.S. midterm elections, according to the report.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Wednesday he had directed the Israeli army and intelligence services to topple the Iranian regime.
"The regime in Iran has still not learned the lesson," Netanyahu told a graduation ceremony at an officer training school in the country's southern Negev desert.
"Mojtaba Khamenei, the current tyrant, has decided to follow in his father's footsteps," he said, referring to the country's supreme leader, who replaced his father Ali Khamenei after he was killed in a U.S.-Israeli airstrike on Feb. 28.

articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: US orders diplomats to depart Saudi Arabia amid Houthi strikes
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: US orders diplomats to depart Saudi Arabia amid Houthi strikes
articles.content_orig:
The US State Department ordered the departure of non-essential staff and family members at its embassy in Riyadh, a move that comes amid intensifying strikes on Saudi Arabia by the Iran allied Houthi rebels in Yemen.
“The U.S. Department of State issued an ordered departure for non-emergency U.S. government employees and their family members in Saudi Arabia,” State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott wrote on X . “Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions.”
While the State Department is drawing down its footprint in Saudi Arabia amid escalating risks, a few other US diplomatic posts in the region are also adjusting their staffing in response to the Houthi threat, a source told CNN.
“This is about the Houthis,” said a State Department official.
The State Department also warned in a security alert on Wednesday that US citizens should be aware of potential attacks on airports and general travel disruptions. That message for Americans came after a series of deadly Houthi attacks in recent weeks have targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi military facilities, oil infrastructure and maritime traffic.
“U.S. government employees working in Saudi Arabia require special authorization from Chief of Mission to use any airport in Saudi Arabia following recent missile and UAV attacks on airports in the Kingdom,” the alert said .
Saudi-backed forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognized government have expanded operations against Houthi positions across multiple frontlines, while Saudi air power continues to provide military cover.
On Wednesday, Saudi Arabia said it intercepted at least seven drones, including one targeting the Shaybah oil field in the kingdom’s Eastern Province, in an attack that killed two expatriate workers and injured two others.
The US has stepped up its support for the kingdom militarily by boosting intelligence and targeting support . But Saudi Arabia has been asking the US for more offensive support, and so far, President Donald Trump has decided against striking the Houthis.
As Saudi Arabia finds itself increasingly under attack, other allies have also stepped up support. On Tuesday, the UK said it will deploy fighter jets to defend Saudi Arabia against Houthi attacks. Egypt also pledged “all necessary and possible forms of support” in recent days.
CNN’s Mohammed Tawfeeq contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: GM aims to leapfrog rivals with new generation of autonomous cars
articles.title_zh: GM aims to leapfrog rivals with new generation of autonomous cars
articles.content_orig:
Cars that drive themselves; virtual assistants that plan a week’s worth of meals and create grocery lists; new-car development processes that speed products to market in half the time. General Motors today gave a wide-ranging overview of how it is incorporating advanced technology into its vehicles and processes.
The first bit of new technology that customers will see is enhanced capability of GM’s OnStar telematics service. OnStar is launching an AI assistant in the 2027 Cadillac Lyriq; that capability will roll out to other models, likely the Chevy Silverado and GMC Sierra next year, and can even be retrofitted to some existing GM cars. In its fullest form, OnStar AI “transforms your car into an intelligent partner,” says CEO Mary Barra.
See all results for Cadillac Escalade IQ / IQL for sale near 95131
As part of this effort, all of GM’s current apps will be rebranded under the OnStar umbrella next year. OnStar moves beyond the car to your mobile devices, and those of your family members that you choose to link to it. All of this would be done with the owner’s permission, of course, and GM reps that we spoke to said the company will not be selling drivers’ data to outside firms—that’s important, given how much more this enhanced OnStar will know about you. It integrates your calendar, and uses previous conversations to learn about the operator and make recommendations.
Chief product officer Sterling Anderson described how the company has transformed its product development using artificial intelligence. What had been a sequential process, from design to engineering to manufacturing, can be done concurrently with virtual modeling, compressing the timeline. As a result, GM claims it can shrink new-vehicle development time to just two years from concept to production. That’s down from four to five years currently.
The company is also employing AI to bring autonomous driving on stream. GM says it will launch autonomous driving on the 2028 Cadillac Escalade iQ/iQL. GM designers are looking toward a single button to actuate autonomous driving, in contrast to today’s Super Cruise, in which the driver must initiate cruise control and then set a speed. The capability will be available first on highways, and then will expand to other roads. “Our vision is that any of our vehicles should drive itself anywhere,” said Anderson. That eventually could be without a driver at all, with the car in what Anderson called “mission mode.”
See all results for Cadillac Escalade IQ / IQL for sale near 95131
This autonomy is enabled by a new central compute platform. Lighter, simpler, and more powerful, it’s being fitted first to the 2028 Escalade iQ/iQL. GM also said to expect it in the Chevrolet Traverse/Buick Enclave/GMC Acadia; the full-size SUVs such as the Tahoe, Suburban, and GMC Yukons; and the light-duty full-size pickups. No dates were given for the new computer platform’s appearance in those models, but we’re told that the changeover doesn’t need to be tied to a major redesign; it can be part of a mid-cycle update. Eventually, the new architecture will expand to all models.
One of the first new-vehicle platforms to fully benefit from the more advanced development process is the upcoming fourth-generation EVs. The Gen 4 EV architecture will feature new LMR (Lithium Manganese Rich) batteries that are claimed to be lower-cost and 20 percent more compact yet still capable of delivering long range. GM says the vehicles on the Gen 4 architecture will be 15 percent lighter than today’s EVs and 25 percent more aerodynamic. The architecture, which GM president Mark Reuss described as underpinning “mainstream EVs,” also features more efficient electric motors and 40 percent fewer parts. Noting that EVs currently comprise a quarter of new-vehicle sales worldwide, Reuss said that percentage “is only growing.” And he added: “GM is committed to EVs for the long term. Even as we offer customers choice today.”

articles.title_orig: What 32,000 Folds Did to the iPhone Duo's Hinge
articles.title_zh: What 32,000 Folds Did to the iPhone Duo's Hinge
articles.content_orig:
Apple hasn't shared iPhone Duo hinge tests or given a lifetime fold number like Samsung, but Joanna Stern used a custom device to subject her review unit to more than 32,000 folds over four nights.
Over the course of the testing, Stern said she thought it might be feeling looser as the number of folds increased, but her final conclusion was that she couldn't feel much of a change. A calibrated push-pull gauge used to take readings before and after the Duo fold test showed the hinge was actually stiffer than before.
But in everyday use, I really couldn't feel a difference. So, after 32,000 folds, it felt pretty much the same as day one, which is pretty darn impressive.
Stern didn't comment on whether the fold test caused the crease to be more visible, which can happen over time with other foldable devices. Her testing was done with a case on, and while the machine opened the Duo flat, it didn't close it all the way each time.
Until Apple shares information on display and hinge durability, Stern's test is all we have to go on. It's unlikely to be the last unofficial folding stress test that we see over the next few weeks.
The full details on Stern's machine, including how it was built, can be found in her YouTube video, and she has more information in her review writeup .

articles.title_zh: iOS 27.2 reveals Apple’s Messages app could soon get highly requested change
articles.content_orig:
iOS 27.2 launches next week , and the update includes code that points to a forthcoming Messages app change: the ability to exclude muted conversations from the unread badge count.
Do you belong to a very active group chat? Or are there people in your life that you prefer to keep on mute in the Messages app?
If either or both is true, it might bug you that muting those conversations doesn’t impact the Messages app’s unread badge count.
Except soon, according to iOS 27.2 code, that might finally change.
Aaron Perris shared the discovery this week in a post on X :
iOS 27.2 RC indicates that Apple is working on a feature to exclude muted chats from the unread count in the Messages app
Personally, I’m very excited by this potential change.
I keep a couple of busy group chats muted inside Messages so I’m not pinged with notifications constantly. And as someone who keeps notification badges disabled for most apps, a red badge is always very noticeable. So it always bothers me when Messages has an unread badge for group chats I’ve muted.
While it sounds like this feature won’t ship in iOS 27.2, hopefully Apple is able to offer it soon.
Would you use this Messages option if Apple provided it? Let us know in the comments.

articles.title_orig: Websites taken down worldwide as critical PHP cyber-security update issued
articles.title_zh: Websites taken down worldwide as critical PHP cyber-security update issued
articles.content_orig:
International governments and agencies have urged websites to address two critical cyber-security flaws in a programming language which powers much of the internet.
The vulnerabilities were found within the PHP programming language, with a fix issued on Wednesday afternoon.
Multiple cyber-security agencies have urged organisations unable to apply fixes in time to consider taking their sites down, leaving bodies such as the Finnish government, Edinburgh council and the BBC to take pages offline.
The flaws were discovered by AI, with cyber-security firm Wiz saying they were the "most severe vulnerabilities ever discovered" by the tech, which is reshaping the cyber landscape.
Finland has temporarily shut down the government's public web services, while the Netherlands' cyber-security agency said it was taking its own website offline due to the vulnerabilities.
The US National Security Agency issued similar advice on X for organisations to take their systems offline if they were unable to update with the fix.
"These vulnerabilities often provide a direct path to the server's file system or database," it wrote.
Meanwhile, the White House said federal agencies were working with leading AI labs to speed up a fix to the issue.
And in a post on X , Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged people to check if their publicly available websites ran on PHP.
The Wikimedia Foundation, which runs the online encyclopedia Wikipedia, said it was addressing the security vulnerabilities.
"We have taken down a number of other systems as a precautionary measure until they can be safely patched," it said.
That led some people to be unable to access parts of Wikipedia on Wednesday.
Edinburgh council's website has also become inaccessible, as well as the online homes for several BBC programmes including Doctor Who and The Traitors.
They have not confirmed a link to PHP - BBC News has approached them for comment.
Other websites, including the art platform DeviantArt, have said they are " temporarily down for maintenance " without specifying the reason.
The vulnerabilities were discovered by cyber-security researchers at the firms Calif and Wiz.
Calif, along with PHP Foundation, were part of a program started by OpenAI called Patch the Planet.
Through that program, they were given access to the AI company's advanced AI tools in order to find and fix flaws in web development language.
OpenAI said in a blog post that the discovery was "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory". It added an internal researcher at the company had also discovered the issue around the same time as the other firms.
The flaws had gone undetected for more than a decade. By August, after a few weeks of using advanced AI tools, they were discovered.
"Frontier models were critical to making this process practical, enabling us to develop and adapt working exploits across multiple applications in hours," Wiz said in a blog post.
It has estimated "roughly 70%" of the internet is affected, though the BBC is unable to verify that figure.
While PHP Foundation intended to release its discovery later this month along with a complete fix for the problem, usually referred to by software developers as a "patch," details of the flaw were leaked on social media on Tuesday.
It forced PHP Foundation to rush out its announcement of the vulnerability and its huge scale.
The Netherlands' National Institute for Public Health and the Environment, an agency of the Dutch government, has taken down its website.
Similarly the website of the Tweede Kamer, the lower house of the nation's parliament, has become inaccessible.
The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), as well as its counterparts in the EU and Australia have urged those who use PHP to apply the fixes.
"Where immediate remediation is not feasible, organisations should consider taking the system offline until it can be fully mitigated," the NCSC said in a note .
Japan's national cyber-security office and EU cyber-security officials have issued a similar warning .
"PHP is everywhere. It ​quietly powers WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento sites, shared hosting platforms, control panels, and an awful ⁠lot of software that doesn't even advertise that it runs PHP under the hood," cyber-security company Huntress said.
Cyber-security expert Don Smith, from the Sophos Counter Threat Unit, told the BBC this would "likely be a priority target" for hackers.
The immediate challenge was not simply installing a patch to fix the issue, but finding and managing every instance where PHP was running, he said.
"The use of PHP is pervasive, it can sit beneath public websites, content management systems, hosting platforms and third-party products, sometimes without even being obvious to the organisation using it," he said.
He said it was crucial that organisations looked out for signs that an attacker "might have already have gained a foothold".
The European Union Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-EU) said the risk scores given to the vulnerabilities "indicate the potential for unauthenticated remote code execution".
Such a cyber-attack could potentially allow hackers to install malware and take down websites.
Dane Knecht, chief technology officer at internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare, said he was "seeing early attacks emerging and are updating mitigations as new vectors show up".
The NCSC said once organisations have installed the update, they should "continuously monitor for security updates from third-party software vendors, including for appliances and services that may bundle PHP".
It is not yet clear which versions of the programming language are affected, but CERT-EU said it could affect all versions of it dating back to PHP 5 onwards - which launched in 2004.
The PHP Foundation has issued the update only for the latest versions however - with people using PHP 8.1 or older being urged to upgrade.
PHP was created for web development. It is used on servers to implement what you see when you visit websites.
Not all websites use it, but it nonetheless powers a large portion of the internet.

articles.title_orig: No more doing dishes or laundry. Airbnb eases cleaning load for guests
articles.title_zh: No more doing dishes or laundry. Airbnb eases cleaning load for guests
articles.content_orig:
Airbnb is changing its house rules, including limiting the cleaning tasks hosts can ask guests to complete during their stay.
Under the new policy, which applies to reservations booked on or after Nov. 20, hosts generally will no longer be allowed to require guests to strip beds, wash and put away dishes or take trash offsite, the company announced on its website .
Hosts can still ask guests to complete simpler tasks, such as placing used dishes in the sink.
"House rules help guests understand what hosts expect, but we've heard from our community that they can be confusing, onerous and hard to manage," Airbnb said in a statement. "So we've redesigned them to make them easier to discover and clearer to set, alongside a new policy that keeps requests reasonable, with no surprises."
The new policy also prohibits hosts from imposing their own fines on guests and limits the use of separate contracts to certain circumstances, including when required by law or homeowners association rules.
Airbnb said hosts can now choose from seven standard house rules and add their own reasonable requests.
The rules will also be displayed more prominently on Airbnb listings, in guests' Trips tabs and in reservation reminders.
Hosts can continue to update their house rules at any time. If a request does not follow the policy, Airbnb said it will flag the issue and allow hosts to appeal.

articles.title_orig: Nigeria's first Ebola patient holidayed in Uganda, officials say
articles.title_zh: Nigeria's first Ebola patient holidayed in Uganda, officials say
articles.content_orig:
Nigeria's first confirmed case of Ebola since the outbreak in East Africa began in May is the wife of a diplomat who travelled to Uganda's capital for a holiday, the head of Africa's health agency has told the BBC.
The woman is originally from Uganda but based in Abuja, where she fell ill three days after arriving home in the Nigerian capital on 3 October, according to Dr Jean Kaseya from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention.
Nigeria's health minister has confirmed to the BBC the 42-year-old patient spent two and a half weeks in Kampala, adding that she also made a two-hour stopover in Ethiopia's capital on her return.
"She's stable, she's improving," Muhammad Ali Pate said.
The authorities were working to prevent the virus from spreading and had identified 44 people who had been in contact with the woman, who tested positive for Ebola on Tuesday, the minister said.
"Not all of them have been in close proximity. We cast the net wide so that we contain it as broadly as possible," Pate told the BBC.
None of the contacts, who are now in isolation, are known to have developed symptoms, including the person the patient travelled with, the health minister said, adding that the woman had not travelled outside Abuja since landing.
Kaseya explained that the woman had first developed symptoms on 6 October when she had sought medical help.
"She went to the first hospital, a private hospital, thinking that she had malaria, and then she went to the second private hospital. She was admitted on the 11th," he told the BBC's Newshour programme.
Malaria is endemic in Nigeria and its symptoms - a high temperature, headaches, muscle aches, vomiting and or diarrhoea - are similar to those of Ebola.
After her condition failed to improve, public health authorities were alerted on Monday 19 October, Pate said.
Her diagnosis was confirmed the next day following three laboratory tests, he said.
The incubation period for Ebola ranges from two to 21 days, meaning those exposed to the virus may not become ill for several weeks.
Ebola is a rare but deadly disease caused by a virus. As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea develop and it can lead to organ failure. Some, but not all, patients develop internal and external bleeding.
The disease spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
The outbreak in Democratic Republic of Congo, which began in May, has claimed at least 4,600 lives, with more than 9,500 cases recorded, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control reports .
Shortly after the outbreak was announced, it was also reported in Uganda, where at least two people died. Uganda declared itself free of the disease in August after its last patient was discharged.
There have been conflicting accounts about the patient in Nigeria and her movements.
Pate and Kaseya's comments contradict a statement issued earlier by the Ugandan ministry of health, which described the woman as a Nigerian national who had gone to eastern DR Congo for business, only transiting through Uganda.
It insisted there were currently no confirmed active Ebola cases in the country and that the woman's passage through Uganda did not mean she had contracted the virus there.
Nigeria's health minister and the Africa CDC chief have sought to play down any tension.
Pate said Nigerian officials were working with Uganda, Ethiopia and the Africa CDC to establish the full facts.
"We respect our sister nation of Uganda," he said. "We have very strong solidarity, we are all in it together."
Kaseya also urged African countries to share information, saying this would help investigators trace the woman's movements and establish where she might have contracted the virus.
And he encouraged Western countries not to impose travel restrictions, saying "collaboration and solidarity" were the way to help stop the current outbreak.
The disease recently spread to Kenya, which has reported at least nine infections.
On Monday, the US advised its citizens to reconsider travel to Kenya because of health risks and raised its travel advisory level for the country.
In 2014, Nigeria successfully contained an Ebola outbreak , which had resulted in 20 confirmed cases and eight deaths.
Pate expressed confidence in the country's ability to repeat that success, citing strengthened disease surveillance, laboratories and thousands of trained epidemiologists.
"Nigeria has muscle memory that has been activated, but we are not fighting the past outbreak in the exactly the same way. We have to be vigilant," he said.
The outbreak in DR Congo has been caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.

articles.title_orig: RIP BioWare: EA shuts down storied RPG studio after over three decades
articles.title_zh: RIP BioWare: EA shuts down storied RPG studio after over three decades
articles.content_orig:
The legendary studio behind series like Mass Effect , Dragon Age , Neverwinter Nights , and Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic is no more. BioWare announced via social media Wednesday afternoon that “after more than three decades of shared adventures, BioWare is closing and early development on the next Mass Effect project is ending.”
The official announcement was posted mere minutes after a Bloomberg report detailed 400 job cuts across BioWare parent company Electronic Arts, including 50 at BioWare, based on reports from “a person familiar with the company’s plans.”
“Across our portfolio, we’re making deliberate choices to align talent and investments where we see the greatest opportunities for players and long-term growth,” EA executives wrote in a message to staff, according to Bloomberg.
Following its 1995 founding in Edmonton, Alberta, BioWare first came under the EA umbrella through a 2007 purchase , before Mass Effect and Dragon Age were even a thing. At the time, EA’s then-CEO, John Riccitiello, called BioWare one of “the most respected studios in the industry” that would “make a strong contribution to our strategic growth initiatives on quality, online gaming and developing new intellectual properties. We also expect this will drive long-term value for our shareholders.”
Of course, EA doesn’t have public stockholders anymore after a $55 billion deal led by Silver Lake, Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, and Jared Kushner’s Affinity Partners took the company private last year. At the time of that move, analysts told Ars to expect “layoffs, studio closures, and [selling] of IP” as the newly private and now heavily debt-ridden company put “a bigger focus on live services, more focus on annual sports franchises, [and] microtransactions” to help increase profits.
In more recent years, BioWare has also been beset by a number of high-profile departures, including founders Ray Muzyka and Greg Zeschuk in 2012 and longtime producer Mac Walters in 2023. Executive producer Casey Hudson, who left BioWare in 2014 , ended up returning in 2017 before leaving yet again in 2020 .
The studio has faced its fair share of troubles following those departures, too, including muted critical and fan receptions for games like Mass Effect Andromeda and Dragon Age: The Veilguard . Anthem , the studio’s attempt at a live-service open-world shooter, turned out more ambitious than engaging for most and was recently shuttered for good well after plans for a sweeping overhaul were aborted .
“What generations of BioWare built together is something to celebrate and remember,” the company wrote in its goodbye post. “These games became so much more because you played them, debated your choices, fell in love with the characters, and made these worlds your own. From all of us at BioWare, thank you for being the most meaningful part of our story.”

articles.title_orig: Energy Dept to loan part of home heating oil reserve to ease prices, drawing bipartisan praise
articles.title_zh: Energy Dept to loan part of home heating oil reserve to ease prices, drawing bipartisan praise
articles.content_orig:
Dagen McDowell warns that the new cost-of-living adjustment will accelerate the Social Security fiscal crisis. She details how retirees face a looming 22% benefit cut by 2032 due to a collapsing worker-to-retiree ratio.
The Department of Energy (DOE) on Wednesday announced plans to loan up to about one-third of the U.S. emergency heating oil reserve in an effort to ease price pressures facing consumers as global conflicts constrain energy supplies.
The announcement indicated that the DOE will loan up to 315,000 barrels of fuel oil from the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve to mitigate supply disruptions. The reserve holds a supply of one million barrels of ultra-low sulfur distillate, which serves as heating oil, at four locations in the Northeast due to the popularity of heating oil as a significant source of home heating in the region.
Under the terms of the DOE's request for proposal, companies that borrow from the reserve in the 2026-27 heating season must return the same volume of oil plus a premium to refill the reserve before the 2027-28 heating season.
"The Trump administration is committed to doing everything in our power to lower energy costs for the American people," said Energy Secretary Chris Wright. "After receiving Senators Collins' and Kings' letter and extensive discussions with Senator Collins, I have directed the Department to exchange barrels from our Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve to mitigate heightened home heating oil costs during the upcoming winter."
TRUMP ANNOUNCES $8B BAILOUT FOR FARMERS TO COVER DIESEL COST SURGE AMID ATTACKS ON GLOBAL SUPPLY
Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the temporary measure should help supplies, but urged New York and states in New England to build a natural gas pipeline. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)
"Of course, this is a temporary measure to solve a temporary supply disruption. I encourage the governors of New York and New England to work with the Trump administration to build the Constitution Pipeline and replace home heating oil with low-cost natural gas. Doing so would save their residents billions of dollars in home heating and electricity costs," Wright added.
Sen. Susan Collins , R-Maine, said in a statement that she is pleased the Trump administration responded to the request to boost the supply of heating oil through reserve releases.
"Approximately half of Maine households rely on fuel oil to heat their homes, and I have repeatedly urged the administration to use every tool to increase supply and lower energy prices. The Department anticipates this release will put downward pressure on home heating oil costs and make a real difference for Maine homeowners as they prepare for winter," Collins said.
TRUMP ADMINISTRATION COMMITS UP TO $42M TO REVIVE STALLED NORTHEAST NATURAL GAS PIPELINE
Heating oil costs have surged this year due to supply disruptions. (Matt Stone/MediaNews Group/Boston Herald via Getty Images)
Collins noted in a press release that the planned release would represent a 13% increase in home heating oil supplies in New England , and should help lower prices as heating oil costs have risen 70% from a year ago.
Sen. Angus King , I-Maine, added that their state "has been hit especially hard by the run up in fuel prices since the beginning of the Iran War and the most obvious example is home heating oil."
King said that Maine is "one of the most dependent states in the country on home heating oil and the cost is absolutely through the roof. This release of stored oil in New England will hopefully be some help."
TRUMP SAYS RUSSIA HAS AGREED TO DELIVER MILLIONS IN DIESEL FUEL AFTER 'HIGHLY SUCCESSFUL DISCUSSION'
Heating oil is a significant source of home heating in the Northeast. (Luke Sharrett/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Releases from the reserve would be completed by Nov. 13 and come from storage sites in Boston, South Portland, Maine; and New Haven, Connecticut.
The volume available per site wouldn't exceed 150,000 barrels, while the minimum offer quantity would be 25,000 barrels. Offerors can submit multiple bid offers, and the process looks to ensure a competitive bidding process in which both fuel retailers and terminal holders can participate.
Bids for the DOE solicitation would be due by next Tuesday, Oct. 27.
