articles.title_orig: Critical GitLab Flaw (CVSS 10.0) Could Allow Unauthenticated RCE Across 12 Years of Releases
articles.title_zh: Critical GitLab Flaw (CVSS 10.0) Could Allow Unauthenticated RCE Across 12 Years of Releases
articles.content_orig:
GitLab released fixes on October 21 for a flaw that lets an attacker run code on a self-managed server without logging in, and it affects every version of the software going back to 7.0, released in 2014.
The fix matters even for administrators who patched nine days earlier: the October 12 update covered only versions 19.2 and later, and the new fixed versions sit one patch above it, so an instance updated then is in range again.
The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-110264 , is rated 10.0 on the CVSS scale, the maximum. GitLab says that, under certain conditions, it could allow an unauthenticated user to run arbitrary code on the server due to an integer overflow during the compilation of a specially crafted regular expression.
GitLab has not said what those conditions are. The company reports no sign the flaw has been used in attacks, and it is not listed in the U.S. CISA catalog of known exploited vulnerabilities as of October 22.
Only self-managed installations need to act. GitLab.com already runs the fixed version, and GitLab Dedicated tenants on the internal releases 19.3.5-internal0 and 19.4.2-internal0 or later already have the fix.
GitLab fixed the flaw in seven versions at once.
The table below pairs each release branch with the version that fixes it.
Four of those versions are older than GitLab normally patches. The company's policy covers the current release and the previous two monthly releases, which, as of today, are 19.5, 19.4, and 19.3.
GitLab said it backported this fix to 18.11.13, 19.0.10, 19.1.9, and 19.2.9 on top of its standard releases, a step it reserves for severe issues.
The reason the flaw reaches so far back is the part of GitLab that failed. The regular-expression compiler is Ruby's built-in engine, called Onigmo, which GitLab ships inside its own packages and patches in its own builds. A weakness in that engine is present wherever GitLab has shipped it, which is every release since 7.0.
GitLab also published two detection rules to help self-managed administrators look for exploitation attempts, named "Onigmo native worker crash" and "Org mode render error burst." They are part of the company's open-source TLDR framework , which writes each detection in the Sigma format against GitLab's own application logs.
GitLab has not said what preconditions an attacker needs to reach the compiler, so administrators cannot yet rule themselves out by configuration; the fix is the only certain protection, and GitLab's advisory offers no interim workaround.
This is the fourth code-execution flaw in GitLab's regular-expression engine that the same researcher, who uses the handle joaxcar, has reported in a month, and the first to reach versions before 19.2.
On October 12 , GitLab fixed CVE-2026-97229, also an unauthenticated 10.0 overflow in the regex compiler, in versions 19.2.8, 19.3.5, and 19.4.2. On September 23 , it fixed two more, CVE-2026-93577 and CVE-2026-89078, both rated 9.9 but requiring a logged-in account. The three earlier flaws stopped at version 19.2; this one does not.
The October 21 release fixes 11 security issues in all, one critical and the rest high, medium, or low.
Two of the others concern authentication. CVE-2026-15723, rated high at 8.2, could allow a logged-in user to take over another account, but only when an administrator has enabled both SAML and LDAP auto-linking.
A cache-poisoning flaw in GitLab's OAuth and OpenID Connect endpoints, CVE-2026-112212, rated high at 7.5, could allow an attacker to redirect certain sign-in flows to a server they control in setups that use a shared cache.
The upgrade carries a cost worth planning for. The 19.4.3 and 19.3.6 releases include database changes that run during the upgrade, and on a single-node server that means downtime while they finish. GitLab says multi-node setups can apply the patch without downtime using its zero-downtime procedure.

articles.title_orig: iPhone Duo's Hidden FaceTime Camera Takes 'Trash' Photos
articles.title_zh: iPhone Duo's Hidden FaceTime Camera Takes 'Trash' Photos
articles.content_orig:
The iPhone Duo 's inner screen has an under-display front camera that's largely hidden from view. It's the first time we've seen an under-display camera on an iPhone, and it turns out there's a reason Apple hasn't used the technology before.
Apple said the camera offers 1080p video recording, but didn't mention photo quality. Gizmodo said it's a 4-megapixel camera and described the photos as "low-res, washed out, and just not sharp at all." It's not good for selfies, and even video calls "look muddy."
Marques Brownlee said the camera is "very first gen" and that the photo quality is "trash." Samsung previously used under-display cameras but dropped them because of poor image quality. Brownlee speculates whether Apple will make the same decision in the future.
Reviewers say the camera is better at video than photos, and it does disappear into the background when you're using the phone, which is a plus.
The ‌iPhone Duo‌ has an alternative 12-megapixel front-facing camera on the outer display, which is much better for selfies, plus with the dual displays, you can use the rear cameras to take selfies. PetaPixel says that if you unfold the Duo and point it at yourself, there's an option to move the camera controls to the outer screen. With that setup, you can use the outer display as a viewfinder for the rear camera to take a selfie.

articles.title_orig: Xbox mandates a four-day return to office
articles.title_zh: Xbox mandates a four-day return to office
articles.content_orig:
Xbox employees close to Microsoft’s Redmond headquarters will need to come into the office more starting in February.
Xbox employees close to Microsoft’s Redmond headquarters will need to come into the office more starting in February.
Microsoft asked its employees to return to the office three days per week last year , and it’s now upping this requirement to four days a week for most Xbox employees. An internal memo, seen by The Verge , describes the change as a “need to create more opportunities for people to work together” after feedback from Xbox employees.
“Starting February 1st, 2027, Xbox employees in Puget Sound who live within 50 commuting miles of Studio D are required to work from the office a minimum of four days a week,” says Jacinda Chislum Pearson, Xbox chief people officer, in the internal memo. “We have thousands of Xbox employees within commuting distance of Redmond. Taking advantage of that proximity and working together in person makes it easier to review work, resolve issues, and make decisions without the burden of scheduling another meeting.”
The change to four days in the office will only apply to those close to Microsoft’s corporate campus in Redmond, Washington, and Pearson’s memo appears to suggest that “established in-office practices” for Xbox studios will remain unchanged.
Microsoft has had exemptions to its return to office rules for certain roles, and Xbox employees with existing exemptions will need to resubmit them again. The return to office changes come just a day after a report suggested Microsoft was planning to announce further Xbox layoffs this month , and in November and January. Microsoft announced in July that it was planning to eliminate around 20 percent of Xbox jobs by the end of its financial year at the end of June 2027.
Xbox is also positioning its updated return to office policy as one that “should be worth the investment” of taking the time to commute into the office, especially for those 40-50 miles away. “Leaders should be present, and coming into the office should not mean spending the same day on Teams calls from a different building,” says Pearson. “Time well spent means reviewing work, solving problems, and playing games together, strengthening our path to becoming one Xbox.”

articles.title_zh: FDA Announces Nationwide Recall of More Than 4 Million Tubes of Toothpaste
articles.content_orig:
More than 4.3 million tubes of toothpaste have been recalled nationwide, including popular children's varieties.
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has issued 17 voluntary nationwide recalls of Brush Buddies, evo and ARU toothpaste products, citing "current good manufacturing practice deviations."
Federal officials did not describe exactly what the issue was.
Related video above |  Recalls explained: How to stay ahead of recalls
The listed products include children’s character-themed toothpastes and several ice cream-flavored varieties, as well as whitening and value-pack products.
Together, the recalls account for 4,301,700 tubes distributed nationwide.
The recalled products include Brush Buddies Barbie and Hot Wheels toothpastes; Crayola Silly Scents bubble gum, watermelon and strawberry toothpastes; My Little Pony bubble gum toothpaste; vanilla, mint chocolate chip, cookies ’n cream and chocolate ice cream-flavored toothpastes; and several mint whitening and cavity-protection products.
Additionally, the recalls include two evo products marketed for whitening and sensitivity; and two ARU toothpastes marketed for gum health and cavity protection.
Click here to view the full recall .
The listed expiration dates range from November 2026 through June 2028.
Pritam International Private Limited initiated the recalls on Sept. 10, federal records state. The products were distributed by Ashtel Studios Inc. of Ontario, California.
The recall is classified as Class II, which means use of or exposure to the product may cause temporary or medically reversible health consequences, but the probability of serious adverse health consequences is considered remote.
Hearst Television has reached out the the FDA for further comment on why the products have been recalled, but has not heard back.

articles.title_orig: SpaceX offers employees 20% extra pay to help bring its Memphis supercomputers online
articles.title_zh: SpaceX offers employees 20% extra pay to help bring its Memphis supercomputers online
articles.content_orig:
SpaceX is offering employees a pay bump to temporarily move to Memphis and help build its data centers.
Elon Musk's rocket company is giving employees a 20% pay increase if they volunteer to spend six weeks assisting its critical supercomputer buildout , according to an email seen by Business Insider.
"We now need leaders — current and emerging — to guide teams and remove blockers as we bring more supercomputers online," read the email, which was sent in early October to all SpaceX employees.
It specified that volunteers did not need to be managers already, adding that construction experience is a plus and that "drive matters most."
Employees who put themselves forward should expect to spend six weeks on-site in Memphis, Tennessee, or Southaven, Mississippi, where SpaceX is currently expanding its huge Colossus 1 and 2 data centers to meet surging demand for its compute business.
Volunteers "must be in good performance standing," with more than one year of tenure preferred, the email said. Employees who volunteer will receive a 20% premium on their base salary or on their hourly rate of pay for the period of their assignment, and be eligible for "bonuses tied to program success."
SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment.
The email described the reallocation of employees from other parts of SpaceX to assist the company's data center buildout as a "surge," a tactic employed by the company to divert employees and resources to mission-critical projects.
In 2022, CNBC reported that SpaceX offered employees pay bumps of between 10%-25% to temporarily relocate to Texas as it attempted to launch its Starship megarocket .
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
The company has been offering "surging" employees a 20% premium on their salary to move to Memphis since at least August, according to another email seen by Business Insider that called for "SpaceX experts and aces" to work for the next three months on the data center buildout. The email said the program is intended to end on December 31, 2026, but could be extended.
SpaceX will cover travel expenses and logistics, both emails said.
The supercomputers in Tennessee and Mississippi, which were originally built by xAI before the startup was folded into SpaceX in February, have become a critical part of the company's business.
In SpaceX's earnings on Tuesday night, the rocket giant said AI revenue that includes leasing out its compute to other companies — including Anthropic and Google — had soared to more than $7 billion, nearly half SpaceX's entire quarterly revenue.
On the analyst call, CEO Elon Musk said that SpaceX was being "hounded relentlessly" by companies looking to rent out its compute, adding that they could have rented it out several times over.
SpaceX has been shifting executives in addition to rank-and-file employees to oversee its aggressive expansion. Business Insider previously reported that the company had placed a former Starship executive in charge of building out its compute capacity in Memphis.
Musk told investors on Tuesday he was also spending most of his time in the city as he looked to push SpaceX toward a target of bringing an extra 10 gigawatts of compute online by the end of 2027.
"I've been spending, personally, a lot of my time in Memphis, often four days a week," the SpaceX CEO said. He previously said he was living in an Airstream trailer on the site.

articles.title_orig: GM aims to develop vehicles in as little as two years with AI, software push
articles.title_zh: GM aims to develop vehicles in as little as two years with AI, software push
articles.content_orig:
NEW YORK — General Motors plans to lean into artificial intelligence and vehicle software for future growth and development amid increasing competition abroad from Chinese automakers and a tougher U.S. market.
The Detroit automaker on Wednesday shared new details about a proprietary AI agent it's releasing under its OnStar brand, plans for a fourth generation of more efficient all-electric vehicles and a target to cut its vehicle development time in half.
GM also reconfirmed that by 2028 , it wants to have eyes-off highway driving, or "personal autonomy," that will let drivers take their attention off the road. The automaker said that technology would start with the Cadillac Escalade IQ EV before rolling out to other, more high-volume models.
"All of these developments are building us the car of the future," CEO Mary Barra said Wednesday during an event laying out the plans, called "GM Forward," in downtown Manhattan.
The initiatives, which Barra, Chief Product Officer Sterling Anderson and other executives discussed at the event, are designed to streamline the automaker's operations, while also improving the capabilities of its vehicles for customers.
"Over the last 12 months, we've evolved how we design, engineer and build our vehicles," said Anderson, who led the event and who has been tasked with overseeing GM's latest technology transformation.
GM said it is now targeting a vehicle development time of roughly two years from concept to production versus a traditional four- to five-year cycle. However, the company did not detail a timeline for reaching that goal.
The event comes as Chinese automakers are growing outside of the U.S. with rapid development times of new technologies and vehicles. Consulting firm AlixPartners said it believes China is currently bringing vehicles to market twice as fast as traditional automakers, with 40% to 50% less investment and a 30% cost advantage.
GM also continues to play catch-up to U.S. EV leader Tesla when it comes to delivering technology advancements through over-the-air updates and automated driving capabilities .
Anderson, a former Tesla executive, declined to speak specifically about how GM's technologies will compare to the EV maker, but said GM's systems will be able to visualize, or see, more things through the use of multiple types of sensors than a strictly camera-based system, which Tesla uses.
He also said the rapid development and new software architecture will help the company better compete against Chinese automakers abroad.
"There's inherent virtue to speed," Anderson told CNBC during an interview after the event. "Not just in being able to get a car out faster, it's being able to develop a system that's far more performant that you could have otherwise."
GM said Wednesday it has major plans for its next generation of EVs and traditional vehicles with internal combustion engines.
The company said those coming vehicles — regardless of type — will have 40 times the computing power and up to 50% faster cellular connectivity than prior systems.
That computing power is expected to help the automaker with over-the-air updates, onboard diagnostics and AI, as well as other technologies such as automated driving features.
The new brain of the vehicle will launch on the $130,000 Cadillac Escalade IQ EV in 2028 before rolling out to other models, including its next generation of EVs.
GM said the forthcoming EVs are expected to be 25% more aerodynamic and 15% lighter and feature electric motors and battery packs that are more compact.
GM President Mark Reuss said despite lackluster consumer adoption and the automaker pulling back billions of dollars in investments in EVs , it remains committed to producing them.
"We continue to develop our future EVs and work to reduce battery costs," Reuss said during the event. "And when the U.S. market is ready for EVs in large numbers, we will be there for them."
GM expects to achieve such targets through the use of AI in research and development.
The company said it is developing a "new operating approach for vehicle development" that leans into enterprise AI and virtualization to increase speed.
"This concurrent engineering model allows us to innovate faster, improve continuously, and scale new technologies across our lineup with incredible agility," the company said in a release.
GM used the development of its next-generation vehicles, including a new battery chemistry, as an example of how the new technologies are reshaping its vehicle development.
The company said it virtually tested more than 300,000 battery designs using its recently announced lithium manganese rich battery chemistry, or LMR, before building a single physical prototype.
Anderson said Wednesday that LMR will be the exclusive battery tech for its fourth-generation EVs. GM had previously said it wanted to use those batteries in full-size electric vehicles such as its Chevrolet Silverado and Escalade IQ beginning in 2028.
Anderson said GM is uniquely positioned to use AI compared to other automotive companies because of its more than 100 years in the industry as well as 30 years of OnStar.
"In the age of AI, data is currency," Anderson said. "For decades, GM's engineering, manufacturing and product teams have generated unparalleled body of data that we're now using to build industry-leading AI tools."
The company is building on its internal use of AI to better shape its experiences for customers.
GM on Wednesday reconfirmed that it plans to launch a proprietary in-vehicle AI assistant through its OnStar technology brand.
The OnStar AI assistant is expected to launch in the coming months on the 2027 Cadillac Lyriq EV through an over-the-air update before expanding to other models.
GM currently uses Google's Gemini for its in-vehicle AI assistant. The company told CNBC earlier this year that the GM-developed AI will be more integrated with the vehicle.
The goal for OnStar AI, which will be available through a subscription, is to help customers be productive while in the car, especially if the vehicle has self-driving capabilities that don't require the driver or passengers to monitor the system.
GM on Wednesday also reiterated its plans to launch eyes-off highway driving in 2028. The automaker said a year ago that it wanted to launch that technology. It's been five years since Barra said she expected the automaker to offer personal autonomous vehicles this decade.
"Our vision is that eventually every vehicle should drive itself or its occupants anywhere, and we're investing across the self-driving stack to make that real," Anderson said.

articles.content_orig:

The U.S. National Security Agency’s sent out an alarming warning on Wednesday that two critical holes had been found in PHP, with patches already issued by the PHP Foundation .
PHP is a server-side programming language so widely used for web applications that it powers roughly 70% of the websites on the internet; by some accounts, that’s more than 33 million sites . It is also used by popular content management systems like WordPress.
The NSA warned that these holes are so severe that if a website can’t be patched immediately, it should be pulled off the web until it can be. The holes allow attackers to infiltrate the server’s file system or a database that may be used by the web app.
Interestingly, these holes have been tucked away in all versions of PHP since version 5, which was released in 2004. Websites not running relatively current versions of PHP will have some updating work to do, as PHP 8.1 and older versions are no longer supported. The recommendation is to update the web server to the current version of PHP, which is 8.5.12.
So how did two such ubiquitous, decades-old flaws that affect nearly every website on the internet suddenly come to light? AI, naturally, particularly via OpenAI and Google’s Wiz.
Security testing company Calif was engaged in OpenAI’s “Patch the Planet” initiative to find flaws in open-source source software. Using GPT‑5.6 Sol, it found one of the flaws, OpenAI disclosed in a blog post . Separately, the Wiz team also used AI, namely its Wiz Atlas security AI agent, Gemini 4 Argon, and GPT-5.6 Sol to find multiple vulnerabilities in PHP.
Both OpenAI and Wiz followed responsible security research practices and worked with PHP on patches before publicly disclosing the flaws. Then they all worked together to flesh out what they found, and test the patches, drawing in a host of others to help.
Wiz thanked Automattic, Akamai, AWS, Cloudflare, Fastly, Imperva, Microsoft, and Vercel. (While WordPress sites use PHP, WordPress has issued a statement saying that the flaw isn’t WordPress specific, and sites running its CMS must patch their servers and work with their web-hosting companies to ensure their sites are protected.)
OpenAI says that these flaws were found by researchers before hackers discovered them. So there were no reports of exploits in the wild. This is also in part because, before AI, these flaws were too hard for hackers to exploit. “With AI this is no longer a barrier. LLMs can help adapt an exploit to different PHP versions, configurations and memory layouts,” Wiz warned in its blog about the flaws.
In other words, this is the kind of security issue that was found and prevented because of AI, but is also a high risk only because of AI.
Now that the issue has been disclosed, hackers are fully in the know. The race is on for the internet to patch tens millions of websites before hackers can attack the unpatched ones. Hence the NSA’s guidance that if you can’t patch your PHP website right away, you’re better off pulling it offline until you can.

articles.title_orig: Saudi Arabia spends billions on its military. Why can't it stop deadly attacks by Iran's Houthi allies?
articles.title_zh: Saudi Arabia spends billions on its military. Why can't it stop deadly attacks by Iran's Houthi allies?
articles.content_orig:
Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia in recent weeks have inflicted severe losses on the kingdom, with missiles hitting energy infrastructure and civilian airports , killing at least 20 people.
The Iranian proxy group has struck the headquarters of Saudi Aramco, the world's largest oil company, and is fighting Saudi-backed government forces for control of Yemen's coastline on the Red Sea, a vital waterway for global energy supplies. The fighting has put further upward pressure on oil and gas prices as Iran and the U.S. fight over the nearby Strait of Hormuz.
Saudi Arabia, despite its size, wealth and a substantial military, has appeared to be on the back foot as it faces the Yemeni rebels. The kingdom's opaque government releases regular statements about Houthi ballistic missiles and drones being intercepted, including five it said were destroyed Wednesday.
But many have got through, including an Oct. 10 strike that killed 13 people at Riyadh's King Khalid Airport, including a U.S. citizen.
"No country can ever have a 100% interception rating, that just doesn't really exist," Elizabeth Dent, a senior fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, told CBS News, but that "was a hell of a one to miss."
Saudi Arabia spent $83 billion on defense last year, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute — far more than any other country in the Middle East , including Israel.
So why has the kingdom struggled to stop the Houthi barrage?
Saudi Arabia is vast and, analysts say, geographically vulnerable.
Its east, home to the kingdom's oil fields, is bordered by the Persian Gulf —   all that separates Saudi Arabia from longtime foe Iran. Early in the war, Iran launched strikes targeting bases used by the U.S. in Saudi Arabia in retaliation for U.S. attacks.
To the north, across Saudi Arabia's long border with Iraq, are Iran-backed militia groups that the Saudis —   along with the U.S. — struck in July in response to dozens of attempted drone attacks on the kingdom's infrastructure and on U.S. installations in the region.
To the south, Saudi Arabia shares a more-than-800-mile border with Yemen. A vast portion of the war-wracked nation is controlled by the Houthis. To Saudi Arabia's west, the Houthis have also been battling for control of the Red Sea's vital shipping lanes.
"Over the last eight months, they have been facing threats from every direction," said Dent.
"There is a lot of critical infrastructure: multiple airports, many pipelines, as well as extensive oil production and export infrastructure, military bases, government buildings, royal palaces, and so on," said Thomas Juneau, associate fellow at the Chatham House think tank's Middle East and North Africa Program. "It is simply extremely difficult to provide air defenses for all these sites over such a large area."
"If the Houthis are able to hit Saudi infrastructure with only a minority of their attempted drone or missile attacks, it counts as a success for them and an embarrassment and a loss for Saudi Arabia," Juneau told CBS News.
Neither Saudi nor Houthi authorities responded to CBS News' request for comment on this story.
The ongoing wars in Ukraine and the Middle East have caused a global supply shortage of the interceptors used to shoot down ballistic missiles and other weapons, including the U.S.-made Patriot system used by Saudi Arabia and other American allies.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, asked about Ukraine's longstanding request for Patriot interceptors, said Tuesday that "every other country in the world" also wants them.
"I also talked to Saudi Arabia today. They'd like interceptors. Israel would like interceptors. We would like interceptors. Every country in the world would like interceptors," Rubio said, calling it "probably the most in-demand product right now in the defense field."
"Demand coming from the international [market] is stronger than ever," Tim Cahill, president of missiles and fire control at Lockheed Martin, the world's biggest weapons manufacturer and maker of the Patriot interceptors, told CBS News last week when asked about the short supply.
Saudi Arabia is secretive about its weapons systems and stockpiles, but CBS News reported in March that Gulf countries were seeking emergency resupplies of interceptors , while the Wall Street Journal and Associated Press have reported that the kingdom has sought air defense systems from Japan, South Korea, France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt.
Patriot interceptors are expensive, costing as much as $4 million per unit .
"If there's fear over utilizing or drawing down your resources," said Dent, "are you more reticent to pull the trigger?"
Saudi Arabia has purchased 730 Patriot interceptors from Washington since 2020, according to U.S. military data , but even if it does have enough, the pricey missiles aren't ideal for combating everything in the Houthi arsenal.
Patriots were designed to intercept ballistic missiles, and the Houthis have launched those at Saudi Arabia. But the rebels also have an array of relatively cheap drones, including weapons supplied by Iran, and locally made copies of Iranian attack drones .
These inexpensive weapons have been a key element in the Houthis' tactics, analysts say.
They can be launched in swarms, Allison Minor, a senior fellow in the Middle East Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told CBS News.
The Houthis "combine an overwhelming number of relatively cheap systems, namely drones, to distract and disrupt and exhaust, and then amid that, also weave in these more catastrophic missile attacks," she said.
The Saudis' multi-layered air defense system is sophisticated, but Houthi drones and cruise missiles can change their trajectory, making them harder to track, said Dent, "so if one aspect of that layered defense system breaks down, it can create a gap in coverage, like what may have occurred for the airport attack."
"This is a whole new ballgame," said Dent. "It's a tactic that requires some adjustments."
One possible solution could be Ukrainian-developed drone interceptors, which cost in the thousands of dollars to manufacture and are produced in the tens of thousands annually, unlike Patriots, which are produced in the hundreds .
Saudi Arabia and some of its neighbors have already made deals with Ukraine to acquire such systems, but Dent said they won't be a quick fix as "a lot of what the Ukrainians have been implementing is very hands-on."
The systems require skilled operators, in other words, and they require training.
Another issue is the Saudi personnel available to receive that training. Analysts do not rate the kingdom's military among the world's best, despite its huge defense budget.
Saudi Arabia's armed forces have a reputation for being "structured and run according to the interests of its royal leadership, with an emphasis on regime security," said CBS News national security analyst Aaron MacLean.
"You can spend all the money you want on your military and your missile defenses, but you also have to have a culture of readiness and excellence among the troops responsible," he said.
"If that's lacking, again, the problem is inherently a hard one: fighting intelligent people who really are trying to kill you and are willing to be quite creative in their pursuit of that goal," he said. "Some shots are going to get through."
Faced with Houthi successes and dwindling Patriots, the Saudis have been "aggressively seeking out air defense support from a variety of partners," said Minor, at CSIS.
The kingdom has invoked a mutual defense pact signed last year with Pakistan and Turkey, under which an attack on one country is considered an attack on all three, much like the NATO alliance's Article 5 . Pakistan has already confirmed a troop deployment to the kingdom, and Turkey is also working toward sending forces .

In the late 1800s, Westminster Abbey clergy stumbled upon a mysterious sarcophagus. The lid was decorated with an 11th-century Anglo-Saxon cross, but the base had a fourth-century Roman funeral inscription. For nearly 150 years, the tomb has baffled experts, but the abbey's consulting archaeologist may have finally figured out who was buried there, according to a new study.
Westminster's chief mason unearthed the stone sarcophagus in 1869, but when experts investigated it, they discovered that the burial had been looted earlier that century. Experts also noticed that the carved decoration on the side of the sarcophagus was stylistically Roman , with a Latin inscription that can be translated as "To the memory of Valerius Amandinus. Valerius Superventor and Marcellus made this for their father." But an enormous medieval cross had been carved into the lid of the sarcophagus, suggesting that the tomb had been reused to bury an important religious figure hundreds of years later.
The mystery of the medieval individual buried in a Roman sarcophagus remained unsolved for 150 years, as no one thought that any bones were left inside. But when the stone coffin was opened for conservation in 2016 and a full skeleton was discovered, clues to the identity of the deceased finally came to light, Warwick Rodwell , the consultant archaeologist for Westminster Abbey, wrote in a study published Wednesday (Oct. 21) in the Journal of the British Archaeological Association .
Although the skeleton had been disturbed over the years, with a hole accidentally made in the skull and arm and leg bones mixed up, it was clear that the person was male, middle-aged, and of average height, bioarchaeologist James Langthorne of Pre-Construct Archaeology wrote in a 2016 report. The man also had some evidence of osteoarthritis, two healed rib injuries and gout. The bones were carbon-dated to between 987 and 1052, confirming that the Roman-era sarcophagus was reused in the Middle Ages.
The Roman-era sarcophagus was reworked in the Middle Ages to include a cross on the top. It is on display in Westminster Abbey.
There is a Latin inscription on the side of the Roman-era sarcophagus in Westminster Abbey.
Archaeologists think that the sarcophagus was originally discovered in the burial pit near the sacristy.
An overview of the interior of the sarcophagus, with the disordered skeleton of a medieval abbot.
The abbot's skull was damaged in the past and then reconstructed using wire and glue before being put back in the sarcophagus.
"This brings us to the final question of importance: who was he?" Rodwell wrote in the study. Despite the lack of grave goods, which may have been stolen in the early 19th century, "he was almost certainly an abbot" who was given a dignified burial in a stone sarcophagus with a large cross, Rodwell wrote.
Based on the birth and death dates of the abbots of Westminster and their tenure as clergy, Rodwell narrowed the candidates down to Wulfsige (abbot from 988 to 993), Ælfwig (abbot from 993 to 1020) and Wulfnoth (abbot from 1020 to 1049). Given that Wulfsige left Westminster to become a bishop elsewhere, he was likely not buried in the abbey.
"Consequently, we have two viable contenders for the occupant of the sarcophagus," Rodwell wrote. "The fact that Ælfwig was already a monk of Westminster might favour him."
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
Although the final resting place of Ælfwig may have been found after a millennium, some questions remain unanswered.
For example, it is unclear why an 11th-century abbot was buried in a recycled fourth-century Roman sarcophagus. The reuse of Roman coffins is extremely unusual, Rodwell noted in the study, and nothing comparable to this sarcophagus has ever been found. One explanation for the reuse may rest with the Latin inscription, whose first word — "memoriae" (to the memory) — suggests that Valerius Amandinus was an early Christian himself. This Roman may have been a significant figure in Roman London, Rodwell wrote, but "unfortunately, nothing is known about his career."
Experts are also unsure where the Roman sarcophagus came from. It was made from limestone sourced from Oxfordshire, a county in the South of England. But perhaps the coffin was originally buried in a Roman mausoleum and they were unearthed and moved at some point, Rodwell noted. But as Rodwell pointed out in the study, "there could be a villa and its cemetery somewhere in the vicinity of Westminster Abbey, awaiting discovery."
The sarcophagus is currently on display in the Queen’s Diamond Jubilee Galleries at Westminster Abbey.
Rodwell, W. (2026). Westminster Abbey's Roman sarcophagus and its afterlife. Journal of the British Archaeological Association . https://tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00681288.2026.2675788

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

articles.title_orig: The Sims Project Rene IS PAUSED – The Sims Project Evergreen / Project X IS NEXT!
articles.title_zh: The Sims Project Rene IS PAUSED – The Sims Project Evergreen / Project X IS NEXT!
articles.content_orig:
ARTICLE UPDATE: The official quote has now appeared on the EA website. Previous references from Variety stated that "Project Lotus is cancelled" however that doesn't reflect the internal memo shared publicly by EA. In the official memo the word "paused" was used.
The video gaming industry has been hit hard today with the latest announcement of the Bioware studio closure. The makers of Mass Effect and Dragon Age are being shut down entirely, and Sims players are probably wondering what this means for the future of their beloved franchise.
We've been reporting tirelessly on the developments of The Sims Project X - and now it appears that EA's executives Cam Weber and David Tinson have confirmed its existence in a mail to staff sent out early today. In their own words (obtained by Variety), The Sims Project Lotus development has been put under Pause. Project Lotus is also a different, possibly internal name for The Sims Project Rene , which is a multiplayer spinoff game made for mobile-first platforms.
Instead, we're getting full focus on The Sims Project Evergreen. Which sounds very much like all The Sims Project X news we've been reporting for more than a year now!
Read the full quote shared on Variety today, later confirmed on the official EA Portal:
Across our portfolio, we're making deliberate choices to align talent and investments where we see the greatest opportunities for players and long-term growth.
In Lifestyle , we’re focusing on the long-term potential of The Sims and skate. We’re going to prioritize our efforts on “Project Evergreen” for The Sims to give the team more time to reach the full potential and vision for the game, and to help make this possible, we’re pausing development on “Project Lotus.” For skate., we’ve had a lot of success in bringing players into the game, and we need to create an experience that keeps them engaged over the long-term. To do that, we are making changes to the studio to have a more focused, smaller team to deliver on a very clear roadmap for our community that we believe will build a healthier and more sustainable business.
The decisions we’re making in our priorities, how we work, and with our portfolio reflect our belief in EA’s future. Some open exciting new possibilities. Others are difficult, especially for the people and teams across the company who are directly affected. In those cases, we will support impacted employees in exploring other opportunities within EA, and we're committed to treating impacted colleagues with care and respect.
We’re sure there will be questions about what these changes mean for individual teams and for EA more broadly. You can speak directly with your leaders to hear more on that, and we’ll make sure to spend time discussing our direction and the work ahead at our next Global Town Hall in November.
The past several months have strengthened our belief in what EA can become. We have extraordinary people, franchises that matter to millions of players, and opportunities to build experiences we've only begun to imagine.
It appears this is the first go-ahead that EA is giving the Maxis team, which is already frightened by their sister studio closing, to go ahead and impress the judges with a new Sims base game.
The Sims insider that's been sharing all The Sims Project Evergreen (or Project X as we called it) gossip had already foretold the shelving of Project Rene and full focus of this single player entry.
According to this same Sims insider, EA has already given the Maxis studio a deadline to deliver The Sims Project Evergreen by September 2027.

Moscow also freed retired US teacher Stephen Hubbard following a meeting between the Russian leader and Trump’s envoy Witkoff
Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to resume US-mediated peace talks with Ukraine as soon as next month, the Kremlin said on Wednesday, after Putin met US envoy Steve Witkoff in Washington’s latest push to stop Europe’s bloodiest conflict since second world war.
The talks in a grand imperial palace in St Petersburg, the ninth time that Witkoff has met Putin in person, began with a goodwill gesture from Russia – the release of Stephen Hubbard, a retired US teacher held in Russia.
President Donald Trump confirmed the release in a social media post, saying the United States was not required to give anything in return.
Hubbard was first detained in April 2022 and was later sentenced to six years and 10 months on charges whose veracity his family and US-based lawyer question.

President Donald Trump’s Oval Office outburst has prompted renewed questions on social media about his mental state .
During a Tuesday press gaggle, Trump repeatedly snapped at Andrew Feinberg , The Independent ’s White House correspondent, ordering him to pipe down , warning him to “be careful” and labeling him a “sick person .”
“Wait, wait, wait, wait. Quiet, quiet!” Trump said while seated behind the Resolute Desk. “What’s wrong with you? Are you a sick person? I actually think there’s something wrong with you.”
Clips of the exchange and other clashes with Feinberg quickly went viral on social media, drawing millions of views and thousands of comments. While Trump has a long history of lashing out at journalists — he’s called them “treasonous,” “stupid” and “nasty” — many users expressed shock at the level of anger on display Tuesday.
“Legit scary,” progressive political strategist Chris Sosa wrote on X. “Trump is a sick man. Literally something is broken,” added Adam Kinzinger , a former Republican congressman from Illinois.
A number of commenters suggested the 80-year-old president was exhibiting signs of mental decline — claims the White House has repeatedly dismissed, countering that Trump is the “sharpest” president in American history.
“If Biden wasn’t fit to campaign, Trump’s cognitive decline should disqualify him from the presidency,” radio host and political commentator Mark Bland wrote in response to a video of Trump barking at Feinberg.
Others specifically raised the possibility of dementia.
“This kind of aggression is a fairly textbook dementia symptom and I’m not sure why we’re not talking about it more,” wrote one X user .
“I have looked after people with Dementia for around 8 years of my life. When I tell you that the way this man said ‘quiet’ paired with the facial expression has made me realise he’s got dementia,” added another .
A third chimed in : “He is exhibiting Lewy Body Dementia symptoms. His demeanor changes at the drop of a hat.”
Trump also had his share of defenders online, including Vice President JD Vance, who later called Feinberg an “ imbecile .”
Feinberg opened Tuesday by asking Trump about his anti-fraud crusade , specifically a new pledge to give whistleblowers 1 percent of the fraudulent funds they uncover. After both Trump and Vice President JD Vance responded, the president asked Feinberg: “Who are you?”
When Feinberg later tried to ask follow-up questions, believing Trump had pointed to him, the president lashed out.
“I don’t know who the hell you are, but you better be careful,” Trump said at one point. Minutes later, when Feinberg mentioned the president’s golf course renovation project , the president growled at him to be silent and called him a “sick person.”
Trump is the oldest person ever to be inaugurated president. And the state of his mental and physical health has been the subject of growing public interest, following episodes of apparent daytime drowsiness , bruising on his hands and swollen ankles .
Multiple health experts have spoken out.
“The president has severe daytime somnolence,” CNN medical analyst Dr. Jonathan Reiner said in May. “And chronic insomnia is a severe illness. It can result in an increase in risk of dementia, a decrease in cognitive effects in older people.”
Last month, Dr. Bandy Lee , a forensic and social psychiatrist who previously taught at Harvard and Yale, described Trump as “an incredibly mentally unstable individual who’s become far more unstable with time.”
The White House has forcefully pushed back against claims that Trump is in any way unwell or unfit to serve.
“If it quacks like a duck, it may actually just be a Democrat hack doctor,” White House spokesman Davis Ingle previously told The Independent .
“President Trump is the sharpest, most accessible, and energetic president in American history and any so-called medical professionals engaging in armchair diagnosis or false speculation for political purposes are clearly breaking the Hippocratic Oath they’ve sworn to,” he added.
The White House has also attributed Trump’s recurrent bruising on his hands to frequent handshakes and said chronic venous insufficiency caused his ankle swelling. In response to claims that the president has fallen asleep in public, the White House Rapid Response account has posted screenshots of news anchors with their eyes closed, insinuating that they had nodded off.
Trump has also insisted he is in excellent health, saying after a May physical that “everything” had “ checked out PERFECTLY .”
Polls indicate a large swath of Americans have concerns. In an April YouGov survey , 48 percent of respondents said that Trump has suffered modest or significant cognitive decline.
The Independent has contacted the White House for comment.

Helen Haines, the Australian MP struck by a car outside her constituency office in an alleged attack on Monday, has had her second leg amputated, her husband has announced.
Addressing the media on Wednesday afternoon, Phil Haines said: “Helen is alive and she’s stable. That is the most important thing for our family.”
Surgeons on Monday had amputated Ms Haines’ left leg on Monday night after she was airlifted to hospital. The 65-year-old was struck twice by a Toyota Land Cruiser SUV outside her electoral district office in Wangaratta in Victoria .
A suspect identified as Brendan Nugent, 43 , faces three charges over the alleged attack on the Independent MP, as police consider bringing additional charges against him. He remained silent during his first court appearance earlier on Wednesday.
Providing an update to the media on behalf of their family, Mr Haines said his wife’s road to “recovery will be long and difficult, but we know she is a fighter.
“She is a determined person who will do her best with our support and love to recover. And that is what we hope for.
“Her heart is huge. She is a very compassionate, caring, loving person, incredibly supportive of all around her; her family, her community, anybody she comes across and her mind.
“We are grateful and thankful that, at this stage, both her heart and her mind are in good shape.”
He said that the couple will celebrate their 40th anniversary in November and, in the last four months, have welcomed four grandchildren.
Thanking the public for the support that has been extended to the family, Mr Haines paid special tribute to first responders at the scene of the alleged attack on Monday, including police, paramedics and the members of the community.
“One thing I’ve learned in the last two days, reinforced by many people, is to take things day by day. I know it’s a cliche, but it’s a cliche for a very good reason.
“So I thank you all for being here. I thank you for listening. And please keep sending Helen your love and our family as well.”
Australia’s governor-general Sam Mostyn said she was “touched” to be invited by Mr Haines to attend the press conference, and also expressed gratitude towards the first responders.
She reiterated that Ms Haines’ recovery would be taken “day by day” after what she described as Monday’s “violent attack”.
She called on Australians to “do what I imagine Helen would be doing if she was not the victim of this terrible attack” and to “not descend into violence and chaos and division”.
The incident has shocked Australia , a country where political violence is rare and politicians have always been accessible to the public. Most MPs and even senior ministers go about their work and personal lives without being accompanied by security teams.
Prime minister Anthony Albanese, who characterised the attack as deliberate, called for a calming of political rhetoric in the wake of the incident, and thanked bystanders for intervening . He also spoke with local barber Ricky Jefferies, who helped detain the suspect .

articles.title_zh: What We Saw at Fast-Track Trials of Riot Suspects in France
articles.content_orig:
Our fall fundraising drive ends Friday, and we’re still 17% short of our goal. No billionaire owners, no paywall, no targeted ads—just readers like you. Can you chip in before time runs out?
French President Emmanuel Macron, whose popularity ratings (at around 18 percent) are well below Trump’s, exited Paris yesterday for the Middle East, even as some neighborhoods of major French cities were still smoking. Supposedly, he is on a mission to bring down fuel prices. Bonne chance to that.
The French mess is best understood in three dimensions that are all connected—the social, the economic, and the political. Socially, the protests, which caught the government by surprise in their ferocity, are mainly symptoms. The most severe riots since the famous events of 1968 began with high school students, who are ostensibly fed up with tattered schools and inadequate materials. But what they are really despairing about is the absence of life chances and hope.
Much of this protest is centered in the French banlieues —the suburbs . In France, where the social meaning of suburb is the opposite of America’s, the banlieues are where the government stashed immigrants and the local poor in massive housing projects that are bleak social failures, while the affluent live in chic city arrondissements .
This story first appeared in our free Today on TAP newsletter, a weekday email featuring commentary on the daily news from Prospect reporters.
No paywall, no programmatic ads — just the reporting. Unsubscribe anytime. Submitting your email signs you up for Today on TAP, our weekday afternoon newsletter.
This social failure is hardly a secret. Several recent hit French films are about seemingly unteachable insolent students and idealistic but quickly burnt-out teachers, beginning with the 2008 classic Entre Les Murs . In the popular TV series, Marseille , starring the great warhorse actor Gérard Depardieu as the mayor, kids in the housing projects do violent errands for the local Mafia.
And it isn’t just students who are disaffected. Just about everyone is pissed at one grievance or another. That’s why the protests spread. The French riots are reminiscent of the old Irish joke in which a man in a pub observes a brawl break out and inquires, “Is this a private fight or can anyone get into it?”
France’s welfare state has reached it limits to compensate for an economy that works only for the rich.
The second, and related, dimension is economic. The French economic model is failing the citizenry, and its failure is a variation of what is occurring throughout the West.
The turn to global neoliberalism since the 1980s has not increased economic performance, but widened inequality. The lackluster growth has put increased pressure on the French welfare state, which is relatively generous. But the welfare state has reached its limits to compensate for an economy that works only for the rich.
As French deficits and debts have increased, the global bond market has raised government borrowing costs, exacerbating the fiscal stress. Interestingly, it is considered a crisis that the French ten-year government bond just hit an interest rate of 5 percent . In the U.S., the ten-year bond sailed past 5 percent weeks ago. But France, as a medium-sized economy, is more dependent on the bond market than the U.S. is.
Macron, the ultimate in technocratic leaders, has tried to trim costs, most recently with a 43 billion euro cut in public spending in his proposed 2026-2027 budget, which includes an increase in the retirement age and cuts in health and other social spending. But these proposed cuts, which are unlikely to be enacted, have only made him more detested.
Politically, these multiple crises, punctuated by protests that in places turned violent, demonstrated the collapse of the political center, and energized the far left and especially the far right. With presidential elections set for April 2027, in two rounds, Marine Le Pen of the Rassemblement National (National Rally) is the front-runner . On the far left, Jean-Luc Mélenchon of La France Insoumise (France Unbowed) cheered on the protests.
Polls show Mélenchon running second, well behind Le Pen. If the final round is Le Pen versus Mélenchon, Le Pen almost certainly wins and by a wide margin. Other candidates on the moderate left and moderate right splinter the rest of the vote.
One outside chance of denying the presidency to Le Pen would be if Raphaël Glucksmann, the nominee of the Socialist Party, continues to gain ground and edges out Mélenchon to face Le Pen in the final round. The latest polls show Le Pen at 36 percent, Mélenchon with 16.5 percent, and Glucksmann 13.5 percent. On the center-right, former Prime Minister Edouard Philippe draws about the same share as Glucksmann.
While the far-left Mélenchon could not defeat Le Pen in the final, Glucksmann or Philippe might well do it. But for that to happen, one would have to withdraw and throw their support to the other—a most un-French sacrifice for the greater good.
The French gains for the far left and the far right are a variant of what is occurring all over Europe, as the center has utterly failed to deliver prosperity and opportunity to ordinary working people and cultural issues have backfired on the socially tolerant moderate left.
In The New York Times, the estimable Steven Erlanger has a smart explainer piece on this dynamic. Complementing his own excellent analysis, Erlanger quotes the Nobel laureate MIT economist Daron Acemoglu pointing out that the traditional moderate left got sidetracked with elite cultural issues and ignored its working-class base. “The centerpiece has to be creating jobs and wage growth and career paths for people without college degrees and diverse skills,” Acemoglu told Erlanger in an interview.
As we used to say in my grade school, No shit, Dick Tracy. I can’t resist adding that when writers in The American Prospect , or our friends at the Economic Policy Institute, keep pointing this out (over decades), it’s not a story. When a prominent mainstream economist finally figures it out, it’s worth a Nobel.
Robert Kuttner is co-founder and co-editor of The American Prospect, and professor at Brandeis University’s Heller School. His latest book is Notes for Next Time: Surviving Tyranny, Redeeming America. More by Robert Kuttner

SpaceX will soon notch a huge spaceflight milestone, if all goes according to plan.
The company will try to catch both stages of its Starship megarocket during the vehicle's next test flight, which is targeted for next month, founder and CEO Elon Musk announced during SpaceX's quarter 3 (Q3) earnings call today (Oct. 20).
If SpaceX succeeds, this "will be the first time that an orbital launch vehicle has been fully recovered," Musk said. "The only way that we can extend consciousness beyond Earth on a sustained basis is with a fully reusable orbital launch vehicle. So this is, I think, a profound technology milestone in the history of civilization and consciousness."
Starship is the biggest and most powerful rocket ever built, standing more than 400 feet (122 meters) tall when fully stacked.
As Musk noted, both of its stages — the Super Heavy booster and Ship spacecraft — are designed to be fully and rapidly reusable, a breakthrough that SpaceX thinks will make Mars settlement and other grand exploration feats economically feasible.
Starship's recovery strategy is different than that for SpaceX's Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy rockets, which are partially reusable. (The latter two rockets have expendable upper stages). Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy boosters come back to Earth on landing pads near the launch site or on ships at sea downrange. Super Heavy and Ship, however, will steer themselves directly back to their launch tower, which will capture each vehicle with its "chopstick" arms.
This will allow SpaceX to inspect, refurbish and refly Starship at an accelerated rate, which is a priority for the company: Musk has said he envisions launching Starship more than 10,000 times per year by 2030.
Starship has conducted 14 test flights to date, and SpaceX has pulled off chopstick catches with Super Heavy on three of them. The company has not yet tried to catch Ship, which is a more difficult proposition, as the upper stage travels higher, farther and faster than the booster does.
Still, Musk is confident that SpaceX will pull off a Ship catch on the first try. (He did not give a specific target date for Flight 15, saying only that it was expected next month.)
"I'd say it's more likely than not that this succeeds next flight," he said. "And if not, we have a steady stream of Starship flight attempts through the end of this year, and and then accelerating next year."
Success would mean back-to-back Starship flights with huge milestones. On Flight 14, which occurred on Sept. 28, Ship reached orbit for the first time ever . It also deployed 26 of SpaceX's Starlink Version 3 satellites — the first 26 members of a next-gen broadband constellation in low Earth orbit that will eventually consist of about 100,000 spacecraft .
The Starship Flight 15 preview was something of an aside during today's call. The event primarily served to announce SpaceX's financial performance during Q3, the three-month stretch that ended on Sept. 30.
And that performance was strong, company representatives said. SpaceX recorded revenues of $14.6 billion during Q3, an increase of 161% from the $5.6 billion earned during Q3 of 2025. The company had a net income of $4.4 billion during Q3, $5.5 billion better than the result from the same stretch last year, when SpaceX lost $1.1 billion.
Just $1.8 billion of 2026 Q3 revenue came from SpaceX's launch division. The vast majority was generated by two other segments — connectivity (services provided by its Starlink megaconstellation) and artificial intelligence (or, as the Trump administration has recently rebranded it, "superintelligence").
SpaceX thinks these latter two segments will continue to boom. That's why it's building the infrastructure to support thousands of Starship launches per year — to loft lots of Starlink satellites and AI data centers to Earth orbit. And the company believes that it's positioned to really start raking in the cash, starting as soon as next year.
"In a nutshell, what this implies for SpaceX annual recurring revenue by the end of '27 is somewhere between 500 billion [dollars] and a trillion," Musk said.
Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. Four playable factions, more than 70 missions, 30 multiplayer maps, The Last Stand and the deepest army customisation in series history. Watch the trailer here . Fight through four complete campaigns, totaling more than 70 missions with branching choices and co-operative play. Command the Space Marines, Orks, Necrons and Adeptus Mechanicus – four distinct factions, each with their own units, mechanics and approach to warfare. Master their strengths as you expand your forces and dominate the battlefield. Take the fight beyond campaign in Skirmish with dozens of customisable settings, four game types and support for up to five AI opponents. Shape the battle, set the challenge and carve your path to glory. Then take the war online. Battle players worldwide across 30 multiplayer maps, three game types and with extensive customisation options that put every variable under your command. Challenge yourself, and others, in the exact way you want to play. Fan-favourite co-op survival mode The Last Stand is back. Team up with two allies and hold the line against relentless waves of enemies. Choose from five heroes and assemble your Strikeforce of companion units, bringing new layers of strategic depth to every run. No matter what mode you choose, make every army your own with the enhanced Painter tool. C hoose from dozens of presets or create your own schemes with colours, decals and war gear. For the first time, Dawn of War IV gives you complete creative control to paint your units’ armour and equipment piece-by-piece. Both editions are available to pre-order now with a 10% discount. The war will continue long after launch. Year One includes free updates featuring the return of Crusade Mode, new maps, modes, Commanders, and the Mission Editor, alongside two major story expansions that will deepen the conflict on Kronus and introduce a new playable faction to the battlefield.

articles.title_orig: Exclusive | Senators Express ‘Grave Concerns,’ Launch Inquiry into Google’s AI Push in Schools
articles.title_zh: Exclusive | Senators Express ‘Grave Concerns,’ Launch Inquiry into Google’s AI Push in Schools
articles.content_orig:
The letter asks Google CEO Sundar Pichai to respond by Nov. 2 on what the company knows about AI's effect on students
Kevin Carter / Getty Images
Sens. Richard Blumenthal, a Connecticut Democrat, and Josh Hawley, a Missouri Republican, sent a letter to Google $GOOGL CEO Sundar Pichai asking what the company knows about how its AI products affect the mental health of kids and their growth as learners, according to The Wall Street Journal .
The senators wrote that they have "grave concern" that Google 's "aggressive push of A.I. products to children in schools is threatening the academic success and overall wellbeing of an entire generation." They set a Nov. 2 deadline for Google to reply.
The letter asks Pichai how much Google understands about the ways its AI tools might harm children, why AI features were made the default setting on school devices, which worries districts, teachers and parents have voiced about students leaning on AI academically and emotionally, and which promotions Google has used to broaden the use of AI in schools.
" Google is forcing their A.I. products into classrooms across America, and children are paying the price," the senators wrote, according to The Wall Street Journal. "We cannot repeat the mistakes of social media platforms where products are pushed onto children putting profit ahead of young peoples' best interest."
The letter cites a September Wall Street Journal investigation. Drawing on more than 60 conversations with educators, school officials, parents, students and clinicians, the investigation found that many students have grown emotionally and academically reliant on Google 's AI tools, according to The Wall Street Journal. The Journal also spoke with current and former Google staff and examined the company's research papers, which showed that Google 's own researchers have cautioned that the technology can carry heightened risks for children and may cause cognitive and emotional harm, according to The Wall Street Journal.
A Google spokesperson pointed The Wall Street Journal to a statement the company issued previously, which read “teachers around the world use our technology every day because it solves real classroom challenges and helps improve learning outcomes.” The statement said Google develops its products by working alongside educators and leaves teachers and administrators in charge of how they are used. Google has said it promotes critical thinking and built safeguards aimed at users younger than 18, among them steps meant to head off emotional dependence, according to The Wall Street Journal.
Slipping test scores have driven a backlash against classroom screen time among people of all political stripes, according to The Wall Street Journal. Parent anger has prompted districts such as New York City and Los Angeles to suspend AI use by students in their classrooms through moratoriums, according to The Wall Street Journal.
Chromebooks make up roughly 59% of the devices in U.S. schools, according to Crypto Briefing . By early October, Google had extended access to its Gemini student hub to every K-12 user on Google Workspace for Education, according to Crypto Briefing.
In a July report, Common Sense Media found that the AI tools built into Google Search, such as AI Overview and AI Mode, present an “unacceptable risk” to kids, according to Crypto Briefing. A Senate HELP subcommittee convened on Oct. 9 to examine how AI is affecting K-12 education, according to Crypto Briefing.

articles.title_orig: Donald Trump Urges UK to Go 'Full Blast' on North Sea Gas After Scottish Gas Drilling Approval
articles.title_zh: Donald Trump Urges UK to Go 'Full Blast' on North Sea Gas After Scottish Gas Drilling Approval
articles.content_orig:
By JAMES TAPSFIELD, UK POLITICAL EDITOR and TOM LAWRENCE, NEWS REPORTER
Published: 02:03 EDT, 21 October 2026 | Updated: 11:57 EDT, 21 October 2026
Andy Burnham was urged to go further in opening up North Sea drilling today after the Jackdaw gas project finally received approval.
The PM defended the decision in the Commons this lunchtime despite a backlash from the Labour Left, Greens and environmental groups.
But Kemi Badenoch insisted that now he had accepted that the move bolsters 'energy security' he should allow more gas and oil licences.
The message was echoed by Donald Trump , who took to Truth Social to praise 'great news' and said the UK should go 'full blast'.
'The UK has started drilling in the North Sea, one of the greatest and most prosperous areas of OIL in the World. They should go FULL BLAST!!! This will make the UK very wealthy again,' the president said.
The Jackdaw project was approved by the previous Conservative government in 2022 but was delayed after a legal challenge by Greenpeace, leaving Labour ministers to decide whether drilling should go ahead.
Downing Street insists a 2024 manifesto pledge against new developments in the North Sea does not apply, as the site was already earmarked.
It is expected to increase domestic gas production by around 6 per cent at its peak, safeguard hundreds of jobs and provide an estimated £2.9billion economic boost.
Tax revenues from North Sea oil and gas will also be funnelled into a new energy wealth fund, backed with an initial £2billion, which will be used to invest in renewable and low carbon projects.
Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh accepted this morning that the development would contribute towards climate change, and said it would not bring down gas prices.
But she stressed it is 'much better' to use domestically produced gas than import it.
The Cabinet minister also appeared to hint that a second project at Rosebank might not be greenlit, suggesting that oil was less relevant to domestic energy issues.
There are claims that some Labour MPs are staying quiet on Jackdaw in the hopes of winning the argument on Rosebank and other Net Zero debates.
At PMQs, Andy Burnham said he had asked the Chancellor and Net Zero Secretary to consider whether the levy - typically around 30p a day - could be removed
The message was echoed by Donald Trump, who took to Truth Social to praise 'great news' and said the UK should go 'full blast'
The Tories said ministers had 'wasted' two years 'faffing' over whether to go ahead
Kemi Badenoch welcomed the move to sign off the North Sea drilling scheme despite a backlash from the Labour Left and Greens
In the Commons, Mrs Badenoch said ministers had 'dithered' for two years over whether to go ahead, insisting if the decision had been taken earlier gas would be heating UK homes this winter.
She demanded Labour repeals its ban on all new oil and gas licences in the North Sea.
'We have the resources, the expertise and the people,' Mrs Badenoch said. 'What we have lost is the confidence to make tough decisions'.
Mrs Badenoch had mocked the lack of cheering from Labour MPs at the mention of the Jackdaw approval.
But Mr Burnham said the Tory government had 'messed up'. 'That's why there was the delay, because they didn't do the process properly,' he said. 'And we've made a pragmatic decision, Mr Speaker, that will allow us to do two things.
'Firstly, build a bridge to a renewable future because the resources that come in now from this decision will allow us to invest in renewables, bring forward clean energy and in this Parliament, substantially de-link gas and electricity prices so that we can bring bills down.
'It will also allow us, Mr Speaker, to do more to help people with bills. I can tell the House today that I have asked the Chancellor and the Energy Secretary (Miatta Fahnbulleh) to look at whether we can remove standing charges from gas bills and to report back to this House at the earliest opportunity.'
Ed Miliband - who was promoted from Net Zero Secretary to Foreign Secretary when Mr Burnham became PM in July, was not in the chamber for the weekly clashes today. He was rumoured to have been resisting the Jackdaw approval, although officials insisted he was busy with the Oman state visit.
Speaking in Aberdeen earlier, Ms Fahnbulleh said: 'The reality is, as we put billions into low carbon energy and we do make that transition, we're going to need gas.
'And, ultimately, if you have a choice between homegrown gas that is on our doorstep that I can make sure that there are conditions in terms of the emissions that come out of that production, or I'm importing that gas or oil from across the world – I think it is much better for us to have homegrown gas.
'It supports our energy security and, critically, it means we are securing jobs here in Aberdeen.'
Ms Fahnbulleh told BBC Radio Scotland of the looming Rosebank decision: 'Each project we have got to take on their own merits and I've got to look at them case by case in isolation.
'But they are two very difference projects.
'Jackdaw is producing gas that predominantly is used in the domestic market, Rosebank is a different proposition because it is oil that is exported.
'So I'll look at it against a series of tests and we'll make the judgment on that at the right point.
'But the decisions are very different and it's important that they remain separate.'
Mr Burnham added: 'At a time when people are really struggling, it's right that we look in a responsible way at maximising the existing energy reserves we have in Britain that could help.
'We're committed to moving towards renewable energy and reaching net zero by 2050.
'But even on our ambitious climate path, we'll still require oil and gas as part of our energy needs for decades to come.
'That's why we're taking a pragmatic approach to the North Sea. We're also establishing a new Energy Wealth Fund to invest in renewable energy, support the green transition and help reduce energy bills over the long-term.
'Our approach will ensure we can boost our energy security, back British workers, ringfence future North Sea proceeds to speed up the green transition, hit our ambitious climate targets and – crucially – bring down bills.'
The PM could be particularly vulnerable on his Left flank, after successfully wooing back a chunk of support from the Greens in recent months.
Zack Polanski immediately seized on the news to accuse ministers of 'climate vandalism'.
'Today's decision by Labour is a betrayal of all of our futures, Labour has abandoned all credibility in the fight against climate change,' he said.
'The Energy Secretary has herself said it will make no difference to energy bills; the Health Secretary has admitted the summer heatwave added to pressure on the NHS, and the industry's own assessment is that it will create only 27 jobs.
'This is a victory for Shell over the people.'
Labour MP Alex Sobel, the head of the Left-wing Mainstream group that helped make Mr Burnham leader, told Politico: 'Jackdaw won't draw gas for many years. Won't make an impact on global prices and will give mixed messages in terms of investment in terms of both renewables and decarbonisation of home heating.'
Nadia Whittome posted on X: 'Approving the drilling of Jackdaw is the wrong decision on every front. It won't bring down bills, it creates barely any jobs, and it undermines our climate commitments.
'True energy security comes from rapidly expanding homegrown renewables, not continuing our reliance on volatile fossil fuels.
